# Parallel degree-two paths give a combined-CS exclusion

Status: ordinary all-size proof candidate, frozen for independent review. These configurations were reducible for the WKE inequality framework in TUZA-19; the argument here proves that they cannot occur in a minimum CS obstruction, with arbitrary outside pages included. No finite certificate is a premise.

## Statement

Let L be a closed link component at a vertex h of a minimum combined-CS failure G. A thread is a path whose internal vertices have degree exactly two in L; its two distinct endpoints u,v may have other link neighbors. Then the following configurations are impossible:

## 1. Boundary-selected reduction and footprint rules

Let U consist of u,v and the chosen thread interiors. Since all interior vertices have link degree2, L[U] is exactly the chosen path union, with at most the extra direct edge uv. Only u,v can have link neighbors outside U.

## 2. Two nondirect threads: the parity tuples

Let their lengths be l1,l2, and let C be their union cycle, of order N=l1+l2. The possible extra edge uv is covered by Q because both endpoints are selected.

### Both lengths odd

Each path has a positive even number of interior vertices. Match those interiors consecutively within each path, leaving u,v unmatched. This gives |P|=N/2-1. Select u,v in Q; they cover the four path-end edges. Select one endpoint of each remaining nonmatching edge, giving |Q|=N/2-1 as well. (The remaining nonmatching interior edges are disjoint.)

### One length even and the other odd

Orient the even path from u to v and match alternating edges beginning at u, leaving v unmatched on that path. Match the interior vertices of the odd path consecutively. The union P has size s=(N-1)/2. Select u,v in Q and one endpoint of each nonmatching edge not already incident with u or v. There are s-2 such edges, so |Q|=s.

### Both lengths even, with at least one length at least4

Choose one of the two perfect matchings P of C by matching from u along the first path and from v along the second. Then s=N/2. The complementary matching has exactly two distinct edges incident with u or v. Select u,v in Q and one endpoint of each of its remaining s-2 edges. Thus |Q|=s.

### Both lengths are2, with uv absent

Here L[U] is C4. Use either perfect matching P and Q={u,v}, selecting the orientation in which both matching edges are path legs. The other perfect matching avoids any chosen f in P. One endpoint of f is an interior vertex. Since uv is absent, no link vertex completes a triangle on f, so the triangle-free variant of the safe-page argument applies.

## 3. The diamond: both lengths2 and uv present

Write the two internal vertices x,y, so L[U] has edges ux,xv,uy,yv,uv. If neither u nor v has a link neighbor outside U, this is a closed diamond component, excluded by the authenticated robustness lemma.

## 4. Direct edge plus an odd nondirect thread

The chosen union is an even cycle C of order N>=4. Match uv and match the even number of thread-interior vertices consecutively, giving a perfect matching P of size s=N/2. Select u,v in Q and one endpoint of each nonmatching cycle edge not incident with u or v, giving |Q|=s.

## 5. Exact reduction scope and provenance

A returning thread cycle becomes a nonempty tree component after its sole branch vertex is removed from the link, contrary to `link_vertex_deletion_cyclic_components_v1.md`. With loops excluded, simplicity permits at most one direct edge per branch pair. Any three parallel paths include two nondirect ones, now excluded. With two paths, the only surviving type is one direct edge plus one even nondirect path.

# Exact packing-cover equality for outside pages on forest bases

Status: ORDINARY_PROOF_CANDIDATE; frozen for independent review. This strengthens the earlier whole-forest minimum-cover corollary by removing minimum-cover optimality entirely. The perfect-graph steps are proved below; no unproved perfect-graph theorem is an input. Those steps are classical, not claimed as new.

## Theorem

Let T be a finite forest on A, let B be disjoint from A, and let F be ANY family of actual triangles of the form uvb with uv in E(T) and b in B. No triangle uses two B-vertices. Let nu(F) be the maximum edge-disjoint subfamily and tau(F) the minimum number of actual graph edges meeting every member of F. Then

## 1. The triangle intersection graph is assembled from bipartite line graphs

Let X have one vertex for each triangle in F, with two vertices adjacent exactly when the triangles share a graph edge. Distinct pages can intersect only by sharing their base uv, or by having the same apex b and bases incident with the same A-vertex a.

## 2. Elementary perfection facts

Call a graph perfect when every induced subgraph has chromatic number equal to its clique number.

## 3. A self-contained clique-cover consequence of perfection

**Replication lemma.** Replacing a vertex v of a perfect graph Y by two adjacent twins preserves perfection. It suffices to prove the coloring equality for an induced subgraph containing both twins; an induced subgraph containing at most one is inherited from Y. Let k be the clique number after duplication. If k exceeds the clique number before duplication, color the original graph and give the new twin a new color. Otherwise k is unchanged and v belongs to no original k-clique. Take a k-coloring of the original graph and let S be v's color class. The induced original graph on V(Y) minus (S minus {v}) has clique number at most k-1: every original k-clique meets S, and none can meet it only in v. Color that induced graph with k-1 colors. The set (S minus {v}) together with the new twin is independent and receives the last color. This proves the lemma, including all induced subgraphs.

## 4. Every intersection clique is an actual graph-edge fiber

Consider a clique of page vertices in X. Its distinct bases are pairwise incident tree edges, because disjoint bases with apices in B cannot share an edge. Pairwise incident edges of a forest have a common endpoint: three edges incident in pairs without a common endpoint would form a triangle. Thus the clique lies in some X_a.

## Role in the weighted TREE question

For a tree component C_i of a minimum ordinary triangle cover, the family of its OUTSIDE pages therefore has exact matching-cover equality, even when those pages alone do not make C_i minimum. This improves the pricing of external pages and is independent of the unresolved internal-triangle collisions in the mixed-Hall selection.

## Attribution and evidence boundary

The replication and clique-cover argument is a classical form of Lovasz's perfect-graph theorem. Original primary publication metadata and abstract were inspected: L. Lovasz, *Normal hypergraphs and the perfect graph conjecture*, Discrete Mathematics2(3) (1972),253–267, DOI https://doi.org/10.1016/0012-365X(72)90006-4. The abstract states the matching-transversal minmax for normal hypergraphs and the complement-perfection consequence. No historical-priority claim is made for the present application. The complete needed graph argument is supplied above rather than relying on an unchecked reading of the original proof.

exact_dependency_and_assumption_lines.text: **Bipartite line graphs are perfect.** A bipartite graph of maximum degree d has an edge coloring with d colors. Add dummy vertices to balance its two parts and add edges, permitting parallel edges, until it is d-regular. Hall's condition follows by counting the d|S| edges from any subset of one part into its neighborhood, which has capacity d|N(S)|. Remove a perfect matching and repeat, decomposing the regular multigraph into d matchings. Restricting the colors proves the assertion. Every clique in a bipartite line graph is a set of edges at one common endpoint, so its clique number is d; every induced subgraph is again a bipartite line graph.

Now let Y be a nonempty perfect graph with independence number alpha. List all its maximum independent sets as S1,...,Sk. Replace each vertex v by a clique of m_v adjacent twins, where m_v is the number of these sets containing v; delete vertices with m_v=0. The resulting graph Y' is perfect by repeated replication and induced deletion. Its vertices can be partitioned into k independent sets, one copy of each v in each S_i, so it has a k-coloring. It has exactly k*alpha vertices and independence number at most alpha, so at least k colors are necessary. Hence its clique number is exactly k.

For a tree component C_i of a minimum ordinary triangle cover, the family of its OUTSIDE pages therefore has exact matching-cover equality, even when those pages alone do not make C_i minimum. This improves the pricing of external pages and is independent of the unresolved internal-triangle collisions in the mixed-Hall selection.

# Combined CS from a perfect actual triangle-intersection graph

Frozen v1, 2026-11-16. Status: ORDINARY_PROOF_CANDIDATE, fresh review requested. This is a sufficient class theorem using actual triangle closure and a classical perfect-graph minmax whose needed proof is already supplied and freshly reviewed in this workspace. No historical-priority claim is made, and no general perfection availability is asserted.

## Statement

For a finite simple graph G, let X(G) have one vertex for every actual G triangle and adjacency when two such triangles share a graph edge. Suppose X(G) is perfect: every induced subgraph has chromatic number equal to clique number. Then τ(G)≤2ν(G), with equality if and only if all nonempty triangle components have literal K4 support. Arbitrary triangle-free background and shared graph vertices are allowed.

## Perfect-graph input at its proved scope

Section3 of `notes/challenger_forest_external_minmax_v1.md` proves that a perfect graph Y has a cover of its vertices by α(Y) cliques. Its self-contained proof uses adjacent-twin replication, then replication counts from all maximum independent sets to find a clique meeting all such sets, followed by induction. It was independently checked in `review/forest_external_minmax_independent_review.md`. No unproved strong-perfect-graph characterization is used here, and the definition of perfection is the explicit graph-class hypothesis.

## Actual clique families cost one or two graph edges

Every Qi is a pairwise edge-intersecting family of actual graph triangles. Such a family either has a common graph edge, or its union is the six edges of a literal K4 and it consists of three or four of its faces. To verify the latter alternative, start with triangles abc,abd. A triangle meeting both but avoiding their common edge ab must be acd or bcd. These three faces supply all six K4 edges. Any further triangle meeting all three either is another K4 face or would need to share their nonexistent common edge; a direct endpoint check excludes an outside vertex. Actual closure supplies the fourth K4 face in G even if it was assigned to another clique.

## Equality forces disjoint literal K4 supports

Assume τ(G)=2k and k>0. Every chosen Qi therefore has a literal K4 support. If two of these supports share a graph edge e, choose for each of those two K4s an opposite-edge-pair cover containing e. Their union uses at most three edges. Use arbitrary two-edge covers for all other supports. Since every actual triangle belongs to some Qi, this covers G with at most 2k−1 edges, contradiction.

## Available role and limits

Any nonclassified graph with perfect X(G) has the integer strict inequality τ(G)≤2ν(G)−1. Literal K5 is outside the class: its triangle-intersection graph is the line graph of K5, whose clique number is four but whose chromatic number is at least five, because each color class is a matching with at most two of the ten K5 edges.

# A crown gives classified residuals, but leaves a simultaneous footprint problem

Frozen ordinary proof candidate, 2026-11-16. This records a different interface for minimum CS, not a general crown exclusion or unrestricted theorem.

## Definition and primary-source provenance

A crown consists of distinct actual graph edges e_1,...,e_r,f_1,...,f_r, r>=3, with actual triangles T_i={e_i,f_i,e_(i+1)}, indices cyclic. Each e_i lies in exactly the two displayed triangles. Other triangles may contain the f_i. The definition and alternating reduction are classical: see Nomoto and van der Pol, Tuza's conjecture for binary geometries, arXiv:2112.06385v2 (23 May 2022), Section3, Claim7.5, which credits Tuza's 1990 crown method. Their all-size theorem is cographic; it is not an unrestricted graphic result. The primary PDF and hash are retained in literature/nomoto_vanderpol_2112.06385v2/receipt.json.

## Independent unweighted reconstruction for minimum combined CS

Let G be a minimum CS failure and suppose it contains a crown. Put q=floor(r/2). Choose q pairwise nonconsecutive crown triangles, for example T_1,T_3,...,T_(2q-1), and call this packing P. Delete all e_i and the q corresponding f_i to form K.

## Why a simultaneous avoidance step is still missing

The unselected f_i remain in K and may lie together in a literal clique block. Avoidance of one edge per block cannot therefore be asserted. A concrete geometric control is the six-crown in the square of C6: the six consecutive-vertex triangles form the crown, the e_i are cycle edges, and the f_i are distance-two chords. Each parity of f_i forms a triangle. Attach a fresh vertex to one parity triangle to make it a K4. Deleting the opposite parity crown packing leaves that K4, so three surviving boundary f-edges are its triangle face. Every K4 triangle meets that face; a maximum K4 packing cannot avoid all three edges simultaneously. This is a footprint counterexample, not a CS counterexample or a proof of minimum-CS availability.

## Statement

Let L be a finite simple graph, let w be a vertex, and suppose F=L-w is connected and unicyclic, while every vertex of L has degree at least two. # Exposable leaves in deficient trees and unicyclic graphs

Status: PROOF_USING_DECLARED_INPUT_CANDIDATE, frozen for fresh review. Source_audit, 2026-11-16 UTC. The ordinary deductions below concern graph matchings, not triangle-packing availability.

## Declared matching structure

Use Gallai-Edmonds with D the exposable vertices, A=N(D) minus D, and R the remaining vertices. Every component of F[D] is factor-critical, F[R] has a perfect matching, and every maximum matching matches A to distinct D-components, matches the R region perfectly, and leaves exactly one vertex unmatched in each unused D-component. In particular

## 1. Leaf counts

**Tree count.** A nontrivial connected tree T with d(T)>=1 has at least d(T)+1 exposable original leaves.

## 2. Retaining an allowed edge

**A.** Let F be connected and unicyclic, with d(F)>=2. If ab belongs to some maximum matching of F, there is a maximum matching of F that contains ab and exposes an original leaf of F.

## 3. Deleting an edge without changing matching number

**B.** Let F be connected and unicyclic, with d(F)>=2. If mu(F-ab)=mu(F), then F-ab has a maximum matching exposing an original leaf of F outside {a,b}.

## Scope and limitations

Connectedness, deficiency at least two, and the stated matching hypotheses are explicit. A bare odd cycle shows that deficiency one cannot simply replace deficiency two in either A or B. This note does not assert that every edge is allowed or matching-preserving, and does not itself construct a WKE pair or establish CS for unicyclic links. It supplies the leaf choices requested for that separate interface. No new novelty claim is made for the matching facts.

# A resilient defect-one graph with a two-edge B deletion has packing at most five

Frozen clarified ordinary proof candidate v2, 2026-11-16. The v1 wording used "connected triangle support" without explicitly distinguishing shared-edge connectivity from vertex connectivity; this v2 makes the load-bearing convention explicit and preserves v1 unchanged. This classifies one exact representation of a near-tight residual. It is NOT a bound for all connected defect-one graphs.

## Theorem

Let the ENTIRE actual triangle family of J be nonempty and connected under SHARING A GRAPH EDGE (one shared-edge-connected triangle component), with tau(J)=2nu(J)-1, and nu(J-e)=nu(J) for every actual edge e. Suppose H=J-F satisfies B for a set F of at most two edges. Then one of the following holds, allowing arbitrary triangle-free background:

## 1. Accounting and whole-pair compatibility

Put m=nu(H), p=nu(J). A new triangle exists, else J would have defect zero. Elementary insertion over B gives p>=m+1. Cover extension gives

## 2. Adjacent restored edges give only K5-e

Write F={ab,ac}. Both ordinary page families must be nonempty. If only one were nonempty, deleting that family's restored base would remove every new triangle, including the possible two-new-edge triangle abc, and leave packing at most m, contrary to resilience. The same applies if both are empty.

## 3. Disjoint restored edges require an intersecting page pair

Write F={ab,cd}. Both families are nonempty by resilience; otherwise deleting the active restored base removes every new triangle.

## 4. The whole new family is a K4

An ordinary ab-page abx outside the four terminals would be disjoint from cda, whose apex a is an endpoint of its base. Such two pages are compatible: any disjoint pair of old spokes in one block would put a and b into that clique, contradicting missing ab. Thus every ab-page must have apex c or d. Similarly every cd-page has apex a or b.

## 5. Ordinary sharp construction and its resilience

Take a root K4 on {a,b,c,d}. Attach one fresh K5 along ab and another fresh K5 along ac, using three fresh vertices for each and no further edges. All actual triangles lie in the three displayed cliques. Delete the opposite root edges ad,bc. The remaining root cross four-cycle has no triangle, so H has exactly the two literal K5 triangle components and is B.

## Exact residual role

The theorem supplies a new finite structural bound ONLY when a two-edge deletion of a resilient defect-one graph with ONE SHARED-EDGE TRIANGLE COMPONENT is already known to be B. Merely requiring the union of triangle-support edges to be vertex-connected would be insufficient: extra literal K4/K5 components may be glued at vertices and would increase packing arbitrarily without changing the defect. It neither asserts that such a deletion exists nor bounds arbitrary near-tight graphs. In particular it does not contradict the previously constructed unbounded near-tight families outside this representation.

## 2. Exact diagonal flip

Suppose a paired book has used spine c and UNUSED red opposite d. Replace its P and Q pages by the two pages on d in the same literal K4. It skips triangle-free input graphs. It does not normalize graph isomorphism or connectedness. Isolates and background edges in an input remain and affect N enumeration. `argv[1]=0` is uncapped. All four stated sufficient crossing regimes are accepted. These are actual generalized packing operations, not a strip-availability theorem. No numerical run or Lean verification was needed.

## Exact replacement and odd-length bonus

The marked setup gives nu(Q)=nu(K)=k and a maximum packing M of L, of size k-1, after deleting the four endpoint spokes. Let D be the literal length-l strip, l>=3, and m=l-2. Write i for selected triangles wholly in D and c for selected outside triangles meeting private D edges I. After deleting these i+c triangles, all retained triangles avoid I and the endpoint spokes; they may use xy, which the new rim packing avoids. Thus all l alternating rim triangles append literally.

## 1. Arbitrary internal rim crossings

For a maximum L packing, let S be the set of permitted internal rim edges used by its outside crossing triangles, and r=|S|. Edge-disjointness and at least one such edge per crossing triangle give c<=r, even if a crossing triangle uses several permitted edges. Internal rim triangles can use at most m-r remaining path slots. Without xy, this gives i+c<=m. With xy, at most one internal spine triangle contributes an extra unit, giving i+c<=m+1. The accepted respective regimes are all lengths with no hub edge and odd lengths with a hub edge. There is no bound on the full outside triangle family, only the exact complete crossing-location condition.

## 2. Pure spoke crossings with independent charges

At an allowed internal vertex w of degree two in the internal path, an outside-used hub spoke prevents internal rim triangles from using both incident path edges: both would need the other hub spoke and would collide. Two outside-used spokes at w prevent both incident rim edges. Since allowed vertices are pairwise nonadjacent, their two-edge incident sets are disjoint. Thus s distinct outside-used permitted spokes force at least s unused rim slots. With c<=s, the same bounds i+c<=m or m+1 follow.

## 3. Even length with a nonisolating rim boundary

A matching F of internal rim edges which avoids the internal path's first and last edges has the required hereditary nonisolation property: after any subset S is removed, endpoint vertices keep their only incident rim edge and every other vertex loses at most one of its two edges. If an internal spine triangle is selected, its apex therefore has at least one still-available incident rim edge, which the spine's two spokes prevent using. The spine replaces a remaining rim slot instead of adding one above them. Consequently i<=m-r and i+c<=m, closing the even-length, hub-present case under this explicit boundary placement.

## 4. One crossing book and local criticality

If all outside private-edge crossings share one fixed private edge g, at most one belongs to M. More generally, the same c<=1 holds whenever the complete crossing family's packing number is at most one. Since i<=m, odd length pays this crossing using the extra uv-page, even when g is an endpoint rim edge or an end-near spoke.

## Availability and the next precise obstruction

The new result genuinely weakens the clean-boundary requirement and pays for selected outside triangles. It needs only the stated marked packing profile and each explicit full crossing-location condition. It does not use defect-two naming, cover eligibility or predecessor resilience to discard crossings.

Frozen ordinary reconstruction candidate, TUZA-26. Independent review requested. This is modular: it uses the newly frozen exact wheel-family classification and, in its last remaining case, the SEPARATE exclusion of degree-four simplicial vertices. That final dependency must be independently established without this cap argument before composing a closed degree-four-cap theorem.

Use the degree-four cap setting inside the conditional minimum Q. The edge uv has exactly common neighbors x,y. The existing cap c has N_Q(c)={u,x,y,z}, with uz absent. Put L=Q-{uv,ux,vx,uy,vy} and A=L-c. The remaining branch has xy eligible in L.

## 1. A private K4 face is an immediate cover payment

Let D be any literal K4 in Q whose complete outside-triangle boundary is contained in the three-edge star at one vertex. The opposite face T is private: none of its three edges is used by any triangle outside D. By whole-triangle eligibility choose a minimum Q cover containing E(T). Remove those three edges and add any two-edge minimum cover of D. Outside triangles remain covered, and all D triangles are covered. This saves at least one edge, contradiction.

## 2. Untouched old cliques have small complete Q boundaries

An old B clique D not containing a wheel rim edge remains a separate literal A triangle component, since all new A triangles are W. It contains at most one W vertex and at most one of u,v. It cannot contain c. If it contains u, it cannot contain x,y,z (the relevant old edges are absent); if it contains v, it cannot contain x,y.

## 3. Freshness and exact possible private-vertex neighbors

At most one old clique occupies each rim edge. Adjacent rim attachments already share their wheel endpoint, so cannot share another vertex: two literal cliques sharing two vertices would share an edge and be the same old component. Opposite rim attachments cannot share an outside vertex a either. Such a shared vertex, together with the intervening rim edge, forms an old triangle using an edge of each clique, merging their old components. Hence all private vertices of the rim cliques are mutually fresh.

## 4. Rim K4 attachments are all impossible

### Along xy

### Along xy

Let D have private vertices a,b. Neither u norv belongs to D. Each private vertex has old degree three and must gain a u/v neighbor. An endpoint outside D has at most one D neighbor, and no private vertex can neighbor both endpoints. Thus, up to labels, ua and vb are present and the other cross attachments are absent.

### Along yt or wx

For D on yt, the old central family contributes only boundary edge yt. The only new bases touching D are uy and vy, each contributing at most one edge incident with y. Thus the COMPLETE Q boundary lies in the three-edge star at y. Section1 gives a cover saving. The wx case is symmetric, with star center x.

### Along tw

If neither endpoint lies in D, its only Q boundary is tw and the accepted small-boundary exclusion applies. Otherwise suppose u belongs to D (the v case is symmetric). The old rim neighbors of x and y in D are respectively w and t; any additional old D neighbor would form an old triangle forcing a missing rim diagonal. The complete boundary is therefore contained in triangle {tw,uw,ut}. The remaining private vertex a is adjacent to u inside D and cannot be adjacent to v, or it would be a third uv common neighbor. By Section3 it has no other outside neighbor, so its Q degree is three, contradiction.

## 5. Rim K5 attachments either are paid leaves or expose degree-four simplicial vertices

For D on xy,yt orwx, both endpoints u,v lie outside D. D has three private vertices, and the two endpoints together can attach to at most two of them. Hence at least one private vertex d has exactly its four D neighbors in Q. It is a degree-four simplicial vertex. Once the independent simplicial degree-four exclusion is established, this case is impossible.

## 6. Final cover contradiction with no old pieces

Then A has exactly W4 triangle support, and L has exactly W4 plus c adjacent to x,y,z. The edge uc and any remaining old edges are background in L. This central six-vertex graph is W5 on rim x-c-y-t-w-x with hubz, plus chord xy.

Background/same-edge wedge reductions -> exact W4 triangle-family classification -> complete Q boundary/freshness analysis above -> K4 payments and K5 triangle-leaf payment -> separate simplicial degree-four exclusion (explicit dependency) -> final xy-ineligibility contradiction. claims.available_statement_verbatim: **Theorem 2.1 (Triangle-deletion criterion).** Let $`T`$ be a triangle of $`G`$ and put $`H=G-E(T)`$, retaining all vertices. If $`\mathcal D(H)`$ is 3-partite, then $`\tau(G)\le2\nu(G)`$. Tuza’s inequality for triangle-3-colorable graphs, including four-colorable graphs, is known from Lakshmanan–Bujtás–Tuza \[[3](#reference-3)\] and follows from Aharoni’s theorem \[[1](#reference-1)\]. The new deduction considered here is the addition of the three edges of a triangle to such a remainder. Merely adding these three edges to a cover loses one unit in the critical case. Equality structure repairs that loss. We use only the specific consequence of Haxell–Narins–Szabó (HNS) \[[9](#reference-9)\] proved below, rather than a classification of all graphical equality cases. There are antecedents for $`K_4`$ equality arguments in planar graphs \[[5](#reference-5)\] and for fractional triangle covers \[[8](#reference-8)\]. The latter concerns $`\tau^*`$, and integer equality $`\tau=2\nu`$ cannot simply be substituted for fractional equality. The elementary intersecting-family lemma below is also known \[[2](#reference-2)\]. No novelty is claimed for these inputs. Liu–Zeng’s preprint \[[12](#reference-12)\] proves the odd-cycle-transversal-three case and the fixed-deficit density range $`c\lt 2`$; our corollaries concern four vertices and $`c\lt 5/2`$, respectively. ## 3. Equality structure and compatible packings **Aharoni’s bound.** Every finite 3-partite 3-uniform hypergraph $`\mathcal H`$ satisfies $`\tau(\mathcal H)\le2\nu(\mathcal H)`$ \[[1](#reference-1)\]. An accessible formulation and derivation also appear in HNS, Section 3, Proposition 3.2(iii) and the following paragraph (author-manuscript p. 9). Thus $`\mathcal D(J)`$ 3-partite implies $`\tau(J)\le2\nu(J)`$. **HNS’s equality characterization.** HNS Theorem 1.1 characterizes 3-partite 3-uniform hypergraphs with $`\tau=2\nu`$ as home-base hypergraphs \[[9](#reference-9)\]. We use the 18 March 2018 author manuscript: Definitions 7.1–7.4, pp. 19–20, and Proposition 7.5, p. 21. The earlier arXiv version has different numbering. HNS permits parallel hyperedges; simple hypergraphs are included. Here are exactly the features of a home-base partition needed for extraction. The partition is denoted $`(\mathcal A,\mathcal R,W)`$: the disjoint pieces in $`\mathcal A`$, the disjoint triples in $`\mathcal R`$, and $`W`$ partition the hypervertices, and $`|\mathcal A|+|\mathcal R|=\nu(\mathcal H)`$. Each $`\mathcal A`$-piece is a truncated multi-Fano configuration on six vertices, containing four distinct underlying triples, any three of which form a loose 3-cycle. For a triple $`R=\{r_1,r_2,r_3\}\in\mathcal R`$, with $`r_i`$ in part $`V_i`$, each auxiliary bipartite graph $`B_i`$ has a matching saturating $`\mathcal R`$. A neighbor $`w\in W\cap V_i`$ of $`R`$ means that $`(R\setminus\{r_i\})\cup\{w\}`$ is a hyperedge. These are consequences of the cited definitions, not additional hypotheses.

claims.available_statement_verbatim: **Lemma 3.1 (Disjoint loose cycles).** If $`\mathcal H`$ is 3-partite and 3-uniform with $`\tau(\mathcal H)=2\nu(\mathcal H)=2h`$, then it contains $`h`$ loose 3-cycles with pairwise disjoint vertex supports. A loose 3-cycle here consists of three hyperedges on six vertices whose pairwise intersections are three distinct singletons. *Proof.* For $`h=0`$, take the empty collection. Otherwise use the HNS partition. Choose a saturating matching in each $`B_i`$, and write $`w_i(R)`$ for the vertex matched to $`R`$. For each $`R`$ the hyperedges ``` math \{r_2,r_3,w_1(R)\},\quad \{r_1,r_3,w_2(R)\},\quad \{r_1,r_2,w_3(R)\} ``` **(1)** form the required loose cycle. Its six vertices are distinct since $`W`$ is disjoint from the central triples and the three $`w_i(R)`$ lie in different parts. Across different $`R`$’s, the same-part chosen vertices differ by the matching property; different-part vertices differ by the tripartition. None belongs to any central triple or $`\mathcal A`$-piece. Thus these supports are disjoint simultaneously; no compatibility between the three matchings is missing. Choose also three distinct underlying hyperedges in each $`\mathcal A`$-piece. These give disjoint cycles, for a total of $`|\mathcal A|+|\mathcal R|=h`$. This is the extraction also used in the proof of HNS Proposition 7.5. Isolated vertices may remain in $`W`$. $`\square`$

claims.available_statement_verbatim: **Lemma 3.2 (Graphical equality consequence).** If $`\mathcal D(J)`$ is 3-partite and $`\tau(J)=2\nu(J)=2h`$, then $`J`$ contains $`h`$ pairwise edge-disjoint copies of $`K_4`$. *Proof.* Apply Lemma [3.1](#lem-cycles) to $`\mathcal D(J)`$. Consider one loose cycle. Name two graph triangles $`uvx`$ and $`uvy`$, where the four vertices are distinct. The third shares with each an edge other than $`uv`$. Its two shared edges lie in $`\{ux,vx\}`$ and $`\{uy,vy\}`$, respectively. They must meet, since they belong to one triangle. The cross choices $`ux,vy`$ and $`vx,uy`$ are disjoint, so the third triangle is $`uxy`$ or $`vxy`$. The union therefore contains exactly the six edges $`uv,ux,vx,uy,vy,xy`$ of a $`K_4`$. Disjoint hypervertex supports mean disjoint graph-edge sets. The resulting $`K_4`$ copies may share graph vertices. $`\square`$

claims.available_statement_verbatim: **Lemma 3.4 (Equality exhaustion).** Suppose $`J`$ contains $`h=\nu(J)`$ pairwise edge-disjoint copies of $`K_4`$. Then every triangle of $`J`$ is a face of one of these copies. *Proof.* An additional triangle $`Q`$ shares at most one edge with each block: two shared triangle edges would place all three vertices in that complete block. Choose in each block a face avoiding its possible shared edge. The $`h`$ chosen faces are mutually edge-disjoint and avoid $`Q`$, contradicting maximality. Extra graph edges belonging to no triangle are harmless. $`\square`$ ## 4. One-triangle restoration and odd-cycle transversals

claims.available_statement_verbatim: **Lemma 4.1 (Two-edge cover).** Every nonempty pairwise edge-intersecting family of graph triangles has a cover consisting of at most two graph edges. The family need not be the full triangle family of its ambient graph. *Proof.* A single triangle needs one edge. Otherwise choose distinct members $`abc,abd`$ sharing $`ab`$. Any member avoiding $`ab`$ must share an edge from $`\{ac,bc\}`$ and one from $`\{ad,bd\}`$. The disjoint cross pairs cannot be edges of one triangle; hence it must be $`acd`$ or $`bcd`$. If there is no such member, $`ab`$ covers the family. Otherwise $`cd`$ is an actual graph edge and $`\{ab,cd\}`$ covers the family. This also gives the $`k=3`$ case of the known intersecting-family result in Aharoni–Zerbib, Propositions 3.2 and 3.7 \[[2](#reference-2)\]. $`\square`$ *Proof of Theorem [2.1](#thm-main).* Put $`h=\nu(H)`$ and $`U=V(T)`$. A maximum packing in $`H`$ together with $`T`$ gives $`\nu(G)\ge h+1`$. Aharoni gives $`\tau(H)\le2h`$. If the inequality is strict, integrality and a cover augmented by $`E(T)`$ give ``` math \tau(G)\le\tau(H)+3\le2h+2\le2\nu(G). ``` **(2)** Suppose instead $`\tau(H)=2h`$. The set $`U`$ is independent in $`H`$, since all three possible edges on it have been removed. Lemma [3.3](#lem-faces) gives a packing $`\mathcal P`$ of size $`h`$ avoiding $`U`$. Let $`\mathcal F`$ be the triangles of $`G`$ absent from $`H`$, and put $`r=\nu(\mathcal F)`$. Every member of $`\mathcal F`$ contains an edge of $`T`$, hence at least two vertices of $`U`$. Consequently every edge of every member touches $`U`$. Every edge of $`\mathcal P`$ has both endpoints outside $`U`$. The single fixed packing $`\mathcal P`$ is therefore edge-disjoint from *all* members of $`\mathcal F`$ simultaneously, and ``` math \nu(G)\ge h+r. ``` **(3)** Since $`T\in\mathcal F`$, we have $`r\ge1`$. If $`r=1`$, any two members intersect in an edge, so Lemma [4.1](#lem-intersecting) gives $`\tau(\mathcal F)\le2=2r`$. If $`r\ge2`$, the three edges of $`T`$ give $`\tau(\mathcal F)\le3\le2r`$. Combining covers of $`H`$ and $`\mathcal F`$ yields ``` math \tau(G)\le\tau(H)+\tau(\mathcal F)\le2h+2r\le2\nu(G). ``` **(4)** This includes $`h=0`$, using an empty packing and no HNS invocation. A graph with no triangle cannot satisfy the stated premise on $`T`$. $`\square`$ For clarity, the choice of packing matters: an arbitrary maximum packing of $`H`$ need not avoid the new triangles. For example, take a $`K_4`$ on $`a,d,e,f`$, add the edge $`bd`$, and then add $`T=abc`$. The old maximum packing $`\{ade\}`$ meets the new triangle $`abd`$, whereas the face $`def`$ avoids every new triangle. Lemma [3.3](#lem-faces) supplies the needed choice.

claims.available_statement_verbatim: **Lemma 4.2 (Four colors give three edge labels).** If $`J`$ is four-colorable, then $`\mathcal D(J)`$ is 3-partite. *Proof.* Identify vertex colors with $`\mathbb F_2^2`$ and label an edge by the sum of its endpoint colors. claims.available_statement_verbatim: **Corollary 4.3.** If $`\mathrm{oct}(G)\le4`$, then $`\tau(G)\le2\nu(G)`$. *Proof.* Choose $`S\subseteq V(G)`$ with $`|S|\le4`$ and $`G-S`$ bipartite. If $`G[S]`$ is bipartite, use two colors on $`S`$ and two different colors on its complement. Apply Lemma [4.2](#lem-colors) and Aharoni directly. Otherwise $`G[S]`$ contains an odd cycle, which on at most four vertices must be a triangle $`T`$. After deleting $`E(T)`$ the only remaining edges inside $`S`$ join the possible fourth vertex to $`V(T)`$, so they form a subgraph of a star. Both $`H[S]`$ and $`H-S`$ are bipartite. Thus $`H`$ is four-colorable, and Lemma [4.2](#lem-colors) and Theorem [2.1](#thm-main) apply. The argument includes all smaller transversals and all configurations on $`S`$. $`\square`$ ## 5. Two-triangle restoration: conventions and reductions For a triangle restored on an independent terminal set $`U=\{a,b,c\}`$, a *page* on the *base* $`ab`$ is a triangle $`abx`$ with apex $`x\in N_H(a)\cap N_H(b)`$. Its old edges $`ax,bx`$ are its *spokes*; write $`N_{ab}=N_H(a)\cap N_H(b)`$ for the page-apex set. Every new triangle is the restored triangle itself or a page. We write $`abc`$ for the triangle on three distinct vertices and $`ab`$ for an edge. A *triangle component* is a connected component of the graph of triangles joined when they share an edge. Packing and covering *slack* means $`2\nu-\tau`$. Let $`T_1,T_2`$ be edge-disjoint triangles of $`G`$. Write $`H=G-(E(T_1)\cup E(T_2))`$, $`h=\nu(H)`$ and $`G_i=H+E(T_i)`$. The individual family $`F_i`$ consists of all triangles of $`G_i`$ absent from $`H`$. The full new family consists of all triangles of $`G`$ absent from $`H`$, including triangles using edges from both restored triangles. Edge-disjoint restored triangles are either vertex-disjoint or meet in exactly one vertex; the latter configuration is called a bowtie.

claims.available_statement_verbatim: **Theorem 6.1 (Exact-equality restoration).** If $`\mathcal D(H)`$ is 3-partite, $`\tau(H)=2\nu(H)`$, and $`H`$ is obtained by deleting two edge-disjoint triangles of $`G`$, then $`\tau(G)\le 2\nu(G)`$. *Proof.* A maximum $`H`$-packing plus $`T_1,T_2`$ shows $`\nu(G)\ge h+2`$. A minimum $`H`$-cover plus the six restored edges shows $`\tau(G)\le 2h+6`$, settling $`\nu(G)\ge h+3`$. Assume $`\nu(G)=h+2`$. Then $`\nu(G_i)=h+1`$, since every $`G_i`$-packing can be appended by $`T_j`$, and $`T_i`$ can be appended to an $`H`$-packing. $`U_i=V(T_i)`$ is independent in $`H`$. Each equality $`K_4`$ meets $`U_i`$ in at most one vertex, so choose its opposite face. The resulting fixed $`h`$-packing avoids all vertices of $`U_i`$. Every edge of a new triangle in $`F_i`$ meets $`U_i`$, so it is compatible simultaneously with every $`F_i`$-packing. Thus $`\nu(F_i)=1`$. An edge-intersecting triangle family with no common edge is contained in the faces of one $`K_4`$. Indeed choose $`abc,abd`$ and a third triangle avoiding $`ab`$. The third is $`acd`$ or $`bcd`$. A further triangle containing $`ab`$ must then be $`abc`$ or $`abd`$ to meet the third; one avoiding $`ab`$ is among $`acd,bcd`$. Such a family can be covered by any chosen $`K_4`$ edge and its opposite edge. A family with a common edge has a one-edge cover. If $`T_1,T_2`$ are vertex-disjoint, no triangle uses edges of both, and two two-edge covers suffice. In the bowtie case let $`T_1=vab`$ and $`T_2=vcd`$. The only mixed triangles are $`vxy`$, where $`x`$ in $`\{a,b\}`$, $`y`$ in $`\{c,d\}`$, and $`xy`$ is an $`H`$-edge. If both $`F_i`$ have one-edge covers, use these and $`va,vb`$. If $`F_1`$ needs two edges and $`F_2`$ one, the $`K_4`$ containing $`F_1`$ has its fourth vertex outside $`\{v,a,b,c,d\}`$: $`vc`$ and $`vd`$ are absent from $`G_1`$. Neither $`abc`$ nor $`abd`$ can be present in $`G_1`$, because it would belong to $`F_1`$ outside that $`K_4`$. Thus each of $`c,d`$ has at most one $`H`$-neighbor in $`\{a,b\}`$, so there are at most two mixed triangles. Include $`va`$ or $`vb`$ in a two-edge $`F_1`$-cover so as to hit one mixed triangle; the one-edge $`F_2`$-cover and one further edge cover the remainder. If both $`F_i`$ need two edges, the cross edges have maximum degree one on both sides. They are a matching of size at most two; choose one endpoint on each side covering the matching, and the corresponding spokes in the two two-edge covers. Again four edges cover all new triangles. Add an old cover to obtain $`\tau(G)\le 2h+4`$. $`\square`$ The proof never needs one maximum $`H`$-packing avoiding $`U_1 \cup U_2`$. The two separate compatible packings establish separate bounds on $`\nu(F_i)`$; the final operation is a cover union. The mixed list is exhaustive because two restored edges from different triangles must meet at their unique common vertex. The argument includes $`h=0`$. ## 7. Restoration with a packing-essential edge **Definition 7.1.** An edge $`e\in E(H)`$ is packing-essential if $`\nu(H-e)=\nu(H)-1`$. The graph is packing-edge-stable if $`\nu(H-e)=\nu(H)`$ for every edge. Equivalently, an essential edge is used by every maximum triangle packing.

A minimum $`H`$-cover plus the six restored edges shows $`\tau(G)\le 2h+6`$, settling $`\nu(G)\ge h+3`$. Assume $`\nu(G)=h+2`$. Then $`\nu(G_i)=h+1`$, since every $`G_i`$-packing can be appended by $`T_j`$, and $`T_i`$ can be appended to an $`H`$-packing. $`U_i=V(T_i)`$ is independent in $`H`$. Each equality $`K_4`$ meets $`U_i`$ in at most one vertex, so choose its opposite face. The resulting fixed $`h`$-packing avoids all vertices of $`U_i`$. Every edge of a new triangle in $`F_i`$ meets $`U_i`$, so it is compatible simultaneously with every $`F_i`$-packing. Thus $`\nu(F_i)=1`$. An edge-intersecting triangle family with no common edge is contained in the faces of one $`K_4`$. Indeed choose $`abc,abd`$ and a third triangle avoiding $`ab`$. The third is $`acd`$ or $`bcd`$. A further triangle containing $`ab`$ must then be $`abc`$ or $`abd`$ to meet the third; one avoiding $`ab`$ is among $`acd,bcd`$. Such a family can be covered by any chosen $`K_4`$ edge and its opposite edge. A family with a common edge has a one-edge cover. If $`T_1,T_2`$ are vertex-disjoint, no triangle uses edges of both, and two two-edge covers suffice. In the bowtie case let $`T_1=vab`$ and $`T_2=vcd`$. The only mixed triangles are $`vxy`$, where $`x`$ in $`\{a,b\}`$, $`y`$ in $`\{c,d\}`$, and $`xy`$ is an $`H`$-edge. If both $`F_i`$ have one-edge covers, use these and $`va,vb`$. If $`F_1`$ needs two edges and $`F_2`$ one, the $`K_4`$ containing $`F_1`$ has its fourth vertex outside $`\{v,a,b,c,d\}`$: $`vc`$ and $`vd`$ are absent from $`G_1`$. Neither $`abc`$ nor $`abd`$ can be present in $`G_1`$, because it would belong to $`F_1`$ outside that $`K_4`$. Thus each of $`c,d`$ has at most one $`H`$-neighbor in $`\{a,b\}`$, so there are at most two mixed triangles. Include $`va`$ or $`vb`$ in a two-edge $`F_1`$-cover so as to hit one mixed triangle; the one-edge $`F_2`$-cover and one further edge cover the remainder. If both $`F_i`$ need two edges, the cross edges have maximum degree one on both sides. They are a matching of size at most two; choose one endpoint on each side covering the matching, and the corresponding spokes in the two two-edge covers. Again four edges cover all new triangles. Add an old cover to obtain $`\tau(G)\le 2h+4`$. $`\square`$ The proof never needs one maximum $`H`$-packing avoiding $`U_1 \cup U_2`$. The two separate compatible packings establish separate bounds on $`\nu(F_i)`$; the final operation is a cover union. The mixed list is exhaustive because two restored edges from different triangles must meet at their unique common vertex. The argument includes $`h=0`$. ## 7. Restoration with a packing-essential edge **Definition 7.1.** An edge $`e\in E(H)`$ is packing-essential if $`\nu(H-e)=\nu(H)-1`$. The graph is packing-edge-stable if $`\nu(H-e)=\nu(H)`$ for every edge. Equivalently, an essential edge is used by every maximum triangle packing.

claims.available_statement_verbatim: **Theorem 7.2 (Essential-edge restoration).** If $`\mathcal D(H)`$ is tripartite and $`H`$ has a packing-essential edge, then $`\tau(G)\le2\nu(G)`$. If in addition $`\tau(H)=2h-1`$ and $`\nu(G)=h+2`$, at least one individual family $`F_i`$ has $`\tau(F_i)\le2`$. *Proof.* Aharoni’s bound on $`H-e`$ gives $`\tau(H)\le\tau(H-e)+1\le2h-1`$. Slack at least two is settled by Lemma [5.1](#lem-elementary), so assume $`\tau(H)=2h-1`$. **Free-page reconstruction.** Put $`e=xy`$, $`J=H-e`$, $`k=h-1`$. Cover deletion and Aharoni force $`2h-2\le \tau(J)\le 2\nu(J)=2h-2`$. Exhaustion gives $`k`$ $`K_4`$ blocks. A block contains at most one of $`x,y`$. If it contained $`x`$ and touched two different e-pages through $`xw_1,xw_2`$, then $`yw_1w_2`$ would be a $`J`$-triangle sharing the block edge $`w_1w_2`$ but not a block face; exhaustion rules this out. It cannot touch an x-spoke and y-spoke because then it would contain $`x,y`$ and the missing edge $`xy`$. Each block therefore touches at most one old e-page, in at most one edge. Cover that block by the touched edge and its opposite edge. If all e-pages touched blocks, these $`2k`$ edges would cover $`H`$, contradicting $`\tau(H)=2k+1`$. Hence some page $`Q=xyw`$ is edge-disjoint from every block. **Hall classification.** Restore a triangle on independent $`U=\{a,b,c\}`$, with new family $`F`$. Let $`N_{ab},N_{bc},N_{ca}`$ be page-apex sets. Different-base, different-apex pages are disjoint, and all other page pairs meet. Thus page packings correspond exactly to matchings between bases and apices. If $`\tau(F)=3`$, every $`N`$ is nonempty (otherwise the other two bases cover F), and no two $`N`$ are the same singleton (their common spoke and the third base cover F). When $`\nu(F)\le 2`$, Hall’s three-set criterion therefore fails only on all three sets: their total union has exactly two elements $`p,q`$. A graph apex occurs in one or three base sets, never exactly two. All sets are nonempty and no two are the same singleton, so both $`p`$ and $`q`$ occur in all three. $`F`$ consists exactly of $`T`$ plus its six pages on $`p,q`$. **Apex-edge forcing.** Suppose $`\nu(H+T)\le h+1=k+2`$ and $`\tau(F)=3`$. Faces of the $`k`$ blocks avoiding $`U`$ are compatible with all $`F`$, so $`\nu(F)\le 2`$ and the Hall classification applies. If $`pq`$ is not an $`H`$-edge, $`Q`$ meets $`U`$ and $`\{p,q\}`$ each in at most one vertex; thus $`Q`$ contains at most one of the six old spokes. Choose two pages on different bases and at different apices avoiding this possible spoke. If the forbidden spoke is $`up`$, take the p-page on the base opposite $`u`$ and any different q-base. The two pages, $`Q`$, and the $`k`$ faces form $`k+3`$ triangles, a contradiction. Hence $`pq`$ is an $`H`$-edge. If $`pq`$ differs from $`e`$, at least two of $`pqu`$ (u in U) avoid $`e`$; they are $`J`$-triangles sharing $`pq`$, hence faces of the same $`K_4`$. That $`K_4`$ would contain two independent $`U`$ vertices, impossible. Therefore $`pq=e`$. **Compatibility and finish.** As in the exact-equality proof, only $`\nu(G)=h+2`$ requires work. If either $`F_i`$ has a two-edge cover, combine it with an old cover and all three edges of the other restored triangle, giving $`2h+4`$. This covers mixed triangles because every triangle absent from $`G_i`$ uses an edge of $`T_j`$. Otherwise both apex pairs are $`\{x,y\}`$. In the disjoint case $`abc,def`$ use $`abx,acy,dex,dfy`$. In the bowtie case $`vab,vcd`$ use $`abx,vay,cdy,vcx`$. These four triangles have disjoint edges. Each old block contains at most one of $`x,y`$, so its face avoiding those vertices avoids all four pages. This yields $`k+4=h+3`$ triangles, contradiction. $`\square`$ Packing-essential means present in every maximum packing, equivalently $`\nu(H-e)=h-1`$. It is not a property of minimum covers. The theorem does not classify arbitrary stable slack-one remainders. ## 8. The unique defective triangle component Two triangles belong to the same triangle component if they can be joined by a chain of triangles in which consecutive members share a graph edge. Components have disjoint edge supports but may share vertices.

claims.available_statement_verbatim: **Proposition 8.1 (Single defective component).** If $`\mathcal D(H)`$ is tripartite and $`\tau(H)=2\nu(H)-1`$, exactly one triangle component has slack one. Every other component consists precisely of the four faces of a $`K_4`$. Thus the triangle family is an edge-disjoint union of isolated $`K_4`$ face families and the full triangle family of a graph $`R`$ with connected triangle-intersection graph and $`\tau(R)=2\nu(R)-1`$. *Proof.* For each triangle component $`C_j`$, let $`E_j`$ be the union of its triangle edge sets and let $`H_j`$ have edge set $`E_j`$. The sets $`E_j`$ are disjoint. Every triangle using edges of $`E_j`$ is an $`H`$-triangle sharing an edge with a member of $`C_j`$, and hence belongs to $`C_j`$. Therefore ``` math \nu(H)=\sum_j\nu(H_j),\qquad \tau(H)=\sum_j\tau(H_j). ``` **(5)** The tripartition restricts to $`H_j`$. Aharoni gives nonnegative integer slacks $`\delta_j=2\nu(H_j)-\tau(H_j)`$. Their sum is one, so precisely one equals one and all others vanish. Equality extraction and Lemma [3.4](#lem-exhaustion) show that each equality component consists of edge-disjoint $`K_4`$ face families. Distinct such families are disconnected in the triangle-intersection graph; connectedness therefore leaves exactly one $`K_4`$. $`\square`$ Edges belonging to no triangle do not affect this decomposition. Theorem [7.2](#thm-essential) implies that an unresolved slack-one remainder must be packing-edge-stable, in particular on its unique defective component. This does not bound that component’s order or classify it by a finite list. Restored triangles may interact with arbitrarily many equality components and with old triangle-free edges; the compatibility arguments below retain those interactions. ## 9. Restoration from flat remainders

claims.available_statement_verbatim: **Theorem 9.1 (Flat-remainder restoration).** If every edge of $`H`$ lies in at most two $`H`$-triangles, then restoring any two edge-disjoint triangles gives $`\tau(G)\le 2\nu(G)`$. No triangle-hypergraph tripartiteness is required. *Proof.* We use Haxell–Kostochka–Thomassé Theorem 2: a $`K_4`$-free flat graph satisfies $`\tau\le3\nu/2`$, and equality components containing triangles are five-wheels \[[7](#reference-7)\]. No planarity assumption is required. **Structural reduction.** In a flat $`H`$ every $`K_4`$ is an isolated triangle component because each block edge already lies in two faces. Remove all such edge supports to get $`K_4`$-free flat $`R`$. Parameters add over triangle components. HKT gives $`\tau(H)\le 2\nu(H)`$. At slack one, $`1=2\nu(R)-\tau(R)\ge \nu(R)/2`$, so $`\nu(R)=1`$ or 2. For $`\nu(R)=1`$, $`\tau(R)=1`$ and all triangles share an edge, which supports at most two triangles. For $`\nu(R)=2`$, $`\tau(R)=3`$ is equality in HKT and precisely one five-wheel remains. At slack zero $`R`$ is triangle-free. No vertex-disjoint decomposition is asserted. **Five-wheel augmentation, complete local check.** Let $`F`$ be a single restored family with $`\tau(F)=3`$ and independent terminals $`U`$. All page-apex sets are nonempty and each pair admits distinct representatives, by the cover argument in Section [7](#sec-essential). A five-wheel $`W`$ retains packing number two after any one edge deletion: in the triangle-cycle of length five, a deleted spoke forbids two consecutive triangles and a deleted rim edge forbids one, leaving two nonadjacent available triangles. If $`U`$ meets $`W`$ at most once, choose two pages on different bases and with different apices, one base avoiding the possible W-terminal. They consume at most one W-edge; append two surviving wheel triangles. If $`U`$ meets $`W`$ twice, these are nonadjacent rim vertices $`a,c`$; write $`U=\{a,b,c\}`$, rim $`a,r,c,s,t`$, hub $`z`$, and $`b`$ outside $`W`$. $`N_H(b) \cap V(W)`$ is independent, since adjacent neighbors would create a nonwheel triangle sharing a W-edge. Consider the page sets $`B=N_{ab}`$ and $`C=N_{cb}`$. If either has an outside-W apex, choose distinct representatives with at least one outside $`W`$: if $`C`$ is the singleton containing the chosen B-apex, choose another B-apex and exchange the roles. This consumes at most one W-edge and the earlier argument applies. Otherwise $`B,C`$ lie inside $`W`$ and are nonempty, not the same singleton. Their possible vertices are respectively $`\{z,r,t\}`$ and $`\{z,r,s\}`$. Independence and absence of neighbors $`a,c`$ force $`N_H(b) \cap W=\{r,s\}`$ or $`\{r,t\}`$; all other subsets make a set empty or make both the same singleton. By reflection take $`\{r,s\}`$. Then $`acz,abr,cbs,zst`$ are four edge-disjoint triangles: their edge sets are $`\{ac,az,cz\}`$, $`\{ab,ar,br\}`$, $`\{bc,cs,bs\}`$, $`\{zs,zt,st\}`$. This verifies the exceptional packing explicitly. **Book core.** Suppose the residual component has $`\nu=\tau=1`$ and other components are $`K_4`$ copies. Choose block faces avoiding $`U`$. If $`\nu(F)\ge 3`$, append three $`F`$-triangles. Otherwise the essential-edge proof’s Hall classification gives apices $`p,q`$. Flatness forces $`pq`$ absent because otherwise $`pq`$ lies in the three old triangles $`pqu`$. Any old book triangle $`Q`$ therefore meets $`U`$ and $`\{p,q\}`$ each in at most one vertex, and has at most one page spoke. Two pages can avoid it as in the essential-edge proof, and append $`Q`$. In both cases packing increases by at least two over $`H`$. **Restoration conclusion.** In slack one, if $`\nu(G)=h+2`$, each intermediate graph has packing $`h+1`$, so the augmentations force $`\tau(F_i)\le 2`$. Combine an old cover, one $`F_i`$-cover and the other restored triangle’s three edges. At slack at least two the old cover plus six edges suffices. At slack zero all triangles are isolated $`K_4`$ faces, and the exact-equality theorem’s elementary four-edge new-family cover argument applies. Hence the full theorem uses HKT and elementary arguments; neither Aharoni nor HNS is needed. $`\square`$ The five-wheel augmentation is the substantive new local step; the book case under a tripartiteness hypothesis is already covered by the essential-edge theorem because a book spine is packing-essential. The flat result removes that tripartiteness requirement and covers the stable wheel core. Its slack-zero portion is the prior equality argument with $`K_4`$ witnesses supplied directly by flatness/HKT. That portion is an application of the equality mechanism. ## 10. Three nonflat star cores

claims.available_statement_verbatim: **Theorem 10.1 (Star-core restoration).** Suppose the nonempty triangle components of $`H`$ are isolated $`K_4`$ face families and one core consisting of a central $`K_4`$ with $`r\in\{1,2,3\}`$ leaf $`K_4`$s attached on distinct edges of a central star, using two fresh vertices per leaf. Then restoring two edge-disjoint triangles gives $`\tau(G)\le2\nu(G)`$. *Proof.* **The core and its parameters** Take a central triangle $`abc`$. At each vertex $`t`$ in a nonempty subset A of $`\{a,b,c\}`$, optionally attach one triangle $`t`$ $`p_t`$ $`q_t`$, using two new vertices for each attachment. Let $`F_0`$ be this triangle cactus. Write $`r=|A|`$, so $`1\le r\le 3`$. Adjoin a hub $`v`$ adjacent to every vertex of $`F_0`$, obtaining the core $`R`$. Equivalently, $`R`$ consists of a central $`K_4`$ on $`\{v,a,b,c\}`$ and $`r`$ leaf $`K_4`$ copies $`\{v,t,p_t,q_t\}`$, one on each selected central spoke $`vt`$. The leaf supports are pairwise edge-disjoint, and each shares just its selected spoke with the central $`K_4`$. Put $`d=r+1`$. Every triangle of $`R`$ belongs to exactly one of these $`d`$ $`K_4`$ copies, so $`\nu(R)\le d`$. The $`d`$ triangles of $`F_0`$ are edge-disjoint, giving $`\nu(R)=d`$. Each leaf $`K_4`$ needs two cover edges, on disjoint supports. A cover of exactly $`2r`$ edges would therefore have all its edges in the leaf supports; its intersection with the central $`K_4`$ is contained in the hub star, which does not meet the central triangle $`abc`$. Thus $`\tau(R)\ge 2r+1`$. Conversely, take all $`r`$ attachment spokes $`vt`$, the $`r`$ leaf-opposite edges $`p_t q_t`$, and enough central edges to cover the central $`K_4`$. This last addition needs one edge if $`r=1`$, one if $`r=2`$, and one if $`r=3`$; when $`r=1`$ choose the central edge opposite the spoke $`vt`$. Hence $`\tau(R)=2r+1=2d-1`$. The core is four-colorable: color $`v`$ with a fourth color, color $`abc`$ with three colors, and complete each attached triangle with the other two colors. Also $`\nu(R-e)=d`$ for every edge $`e`$. If $`e`$ is a hub spoke, the $`F_0`$ triangles avoid it. If $`e`$ is an $`F_0`$ edge, replace its $`F_0`$ triangle by a hub face of its $`K_4`$ avoiding $`e`$ and retain all other $`F_0`$ triangles. Thus none of the cores has a packing-essential edge. **Two-edge avoidance** Let $`f,g`$ be $`F_0`$ edges in different triangle blocks of $`F_0`$. There is a $`d`$-triangle packing of $`R`$ avoiding both, except possibly when one is a central edge and one is in a leaf block, and both edges are opposite that leaf’s attachment vertex. To prove the assertion, retain every unaffected $`F_0`$ triangle. Replace the two affected triangles by hub faces avoiding their forbidden edges. For two different leaf blocks the possible hub spokes belong to disjoint sets of nonhub vertices, so any choices are compatible. For a central block and a leaf at $`t`$, the only possible shared spoke is $`vt`$. A hub face avoiding a forbidden edge can avoid $`vt`$ as well unless that edge is opposite $`t`$ in its block. Unless both forbidden edges are opposite $`t`$, make at least one of the two face choices avoid $`vt`$. This yields the desired packing. **Single restoration** Suppose $`H`$ has triangle components consisting of any $`k`$ isolated $`K_4`$ face components and one isolated copy of $`R`$. Additional edges belonging to no triangle are allowed. Let $`U`$ be independent in $`H`$, with $`|U|=3`$; restore $`T`$ on $`U`$ and let $`F`$ be the new triangle family. Then ``` math \tau(F)=3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \nu(H+E(T))\ge\nu(H)+2. ``` **(6)** It suffices to find $`d+2`$ compatible triangles from $`R`$ and $`F`$. Indeed, one face in each of the other $`k`$ $`K_4`$ copies can be chosen to avoid $`U`$, and these faces are compatible with every $`F`$-triangle and with $`R`$. The isolated copy of $`R`$ is induced on its vertices: any additional edge between two nonhub vertices would form a new hub triangle sharing an R-spoke, contrary to isolation. Its listed neighborhoods can therefore be used as $`H`$-neighborhoods restricted to $`R`$. We repeatedly use the elementary fact that $`\tau(F)=3`$ forces each base edge of $`T`$ to have a nonempty page-apex set, and any two of these sets have distinct representatives. If two sets were the same singleton, the common spoke and the third base edge would cover $`F`$. **At most one vertex of $`U`$ in $`R`$.** Choose two pages with distinct apices, one whose base avoids the possible R-vertex and one on a different base. The first uses no $`R`$-edge and the second at most one. Since $`\nu(R-e)=d`$, these two pages are compatible with a $`d`$-packing of $`R`$. **Exactly two vertices of $`U`$ in $`R`$.** Write $`U=\{u,w,z\}`$, where $`u,w`$ are nonadjacent vertices of $`R`$ and $`z`$ lies outside $`R`$. Let $`B`$ and $`C`$ be the common-neighbor sets in $`H`$ for uz and wz. They are nonempty and admit distinct representatives. If either contains an apex outside $`R`$, choose distinct representatives $`b`$ in $`B`$ and $`c`$ in $`C`$ with at most one in $`R`$. The two pages $`uzb,wzc`$ consume at most one $`R`$-edge between them, and a $`d`$-packing survives. Otherwise both $`B`$ and $`C`$ lie in $`R`$. Since the $`R`$ triangle component is isolated, $`N_H(z) \cap V(R)`$ is independent in $`R`$: an adjacent pair there would give a new $`H`$-triangle on an $`R`$-edge. If this neighborhood contained the hub $`v`$, it would contain no other R-vertex, forcing $`B=C=\{v\}`$, which is excluded. Thus distinct $`b`$ in $`B,c`$ in $`C`$ lie in $`F_0`$. The pages $`uzb,wzc`$ use the $`F_0`$ edges $`ub,wc`$. These edges lie in different $`F_0`$ triangle blocks because $`u,w`$ are nonadjacent. Apply the two-edge avoidance fact. If its exception does not occur, the two pages and a $`d`$-packing of $`R`$ suffice. In the exceptional case, relabel the central triangle as $`abc`$ and the exceptional leaf as $`b`$ $`p`$ $`q`$ so that $`u=a,w=p`$, and the two selected page apices are $`c,q`$. (Symmetry permits exchanging the two terminals and the two endpoints of either opposite edge.) Besides the two pages $`azc,pzq`$, the third page $`apb`$ exists, because $`ab`$ and $`pb`$ are $`R`$-edges. The three pages ``` math azc,\quad pzq,\quad apb ``` **(7)** are edge-disjoint. Omit the central $`F_0`$ triangle, replace the leaf $`bpq`$ by the hub face $`vbq`$, and retain every other leaf triangle. These $`d-1`$ old triangles are compatible with all three pages and with each other. Their total is $`d+2`$. **All three vertices of $`U`$ in $`R`$.** The hub $`v`$ is not in $`U`$. If there is any page with an apex outside $`R`$, combine it with a page on a different base having apex $`v`$. These two pages are edge-disjoint; their $`R`$-edges, if any, are hub spokes. They are therefore compatible with all $`d`$ triangles of $`F_0`$. Assume all page apices lie in $`R`$. An independent triple of $`F_0`$ contains at most one central vertex and at most one private vertex from each leaf. If it contains no central vertex, its members lie in three distinct leaves and have no common neighbors in $`F_0`$; all their page apices are just $`v`$. This gives a two-edge cover of $`F`$, contrary to $`\tau(F)=3`$. Thus, after relabeling, $`U=\{a,p_b,p_c\}`$, where $`p_b`$ and $`p_c`$ are private vertices of the leaves at $`b`$ and $`c`$. The three pages ``` math a p_b b,\quad a p_c c,\quad p_b p_c v ``` **(8)** are edge-disjoint. Omit the central triangle $`abc`$; replace the b-leaf by $`vbq_b`$ and the c-leaf by $`vcq_c`$; retain the a-leaf triangle if it exists. These $`d-1`$ old triangles are edge-disjoint and compatible with the three pages. Again the total is $`d+2`$. This completes the lemma. **Completion of the proof** Let $`T_1,T_2`$ be arbitrary edge-disjoint restored triangles whose deletion leaves $`H`$ as above. Write $`h=\nu(H)=k+d`$. Then $`\tau(H)=2h-1`$. If $`\nu(G)\ge h+3`$, the old cover plus the six restored edges suffices. Otherwise $`\nu(G)=h+2`$ and every individual intermediate graph has packing number at most $`h+1`$. The lemma forces $`\tau(F_i)\le 2`$ for both $`i`$. An old cover, one such two-edge cover, and the three edges of the other restored triangle cover $`G`$, mixed triangles included, with at most $`2h+4`$ edges. Hence Tuza’s inequality holds for two-triangle restoration from any remainder whose triangle components are isolated $`K_4`$ copies plus one of these three $`K_4`$-star cores. The $`r=1`$ case is the two-$`K_4`$ shared-edge core. The $`r=2`$ and $`r=3`$ cases are additional nonflat, packing-edge-stable examples. This is not a classification of every near-equality remainder. $`\square`$ ## 11. Closed-boundary deletion and stability

claims.available_statement_verbatim: **Theorem 11.1 (Closed-boundary equality deletion).** Suppose $`\mathcal D(H)`$ is 3-partite, $`\nu(H)=h`$, $`\tau(H)=2h-1`$. Let $`U,P`$ be disjoint independent graph-vertex sets, $`W=U \cup P`$. Assume that for every **actual $`H`$-edge** $`px`$ with $`p`$ in $`P`$ and $`x`$ outside $`W`$, at most one vertex of $`U`$ is adjacent in $`H`$ to both $`p`$ and $`x`$. Let A be any subset of $`E_H(U,P)`$, without any cardinality bound. If $`K=H-A`$ has $`\tau(K)=2\nu(K)`$, then $`H`$ has a packing-essential edge. Consequently, if $`H`$ is packing-edge-stable, every such A satisfies ``` math \begin{gathered} \nu(H-A) \ge h-\lfloor |A|/2\rfloor \end{gathered} ``` **(9)** Independence of $`P`$ and the local uniqueness condition are both retained hypotheses; no theorem without them is asserted. The condition is not asserted automatically for the union of two restoration boundaries. *Proof.* Let $`L`$ be all $`H`$-triangles absent from $`K`$. A triangle containing $`up`$ in A cannot have its third vertex in $`U`$ or $`P`$ because both are independent. Thus every L-triangle is $`upx`$ with $`u`$ in $`U`$, $`p`$ in $`P`$, $`x`$ outside $`W`$, and it contains exactly one A-edge. Write $`k=\nu(K)`$. In an equality $`K_4`$ there are at most two $`W`$ vertices, at most one from each independent side. If there are at most one, select a face avoiding $`W`$. Its edges have both endpoints outside $`W`$, whereas every edge in an L-triangle meets $`W`$. If there are two, call them $`u,p`$ and write the block $`upxy`$. The edge $`up`$ survives, hence is not in A. Select $`pxy`$. The edge $`xy`$ cannot lie in $`L`$. If $`px`$ lay in a lost triangle $`ptx`$, then $`t`$ is in $`U`$ and $`pt`$ is in A. The actual edge $`px`$ has both $`u`$ and $`t`$ as common U-neighbors, so $`t=u`$, contradicting that $`up`$ survives. The same handles $`py`$. Put $`K=H-A`$, and suppose ``` math \begin{gathered} \nu(K)=h-d, \tau(K)=2(h-d)-1 \end{gathered} ``` **(11)** Let $`L_A`$ be the **full** family of $`H`$-triangles using A, including triangles that might also use an edge $`g`$ considered later. If $`\nu(L_A)\ge d+2`$, then $`K`$ is packing-edge-stable. *Proof.* If $`g`$ were essential in $`K`$, then $`J=K-g`$ has $`\nu(J)=h-d-1`$. The one-edge cover-loss bound gives $`\tau(J)\ge 2(h-d)-2`$, and Aharoni gives the reverse inequality. Thus $`J`$ is equality. The face-selection proof in Section [11](#sec-boundary) applies to every $`J`$ block with respect to the original $`H,U,P,A`$: a retained $`up`$ is still outside A, and local uniqueness is a statement about $`H`$. This proof needs no hypothesis $`\tau(H)=2h-1`$ and does not use the integrality of $`L_A`$. A sufficient row condition is that at least $`d+2`$ $`U`$ rows contain an A-edge lying in an $`H`$-triangle. claims.available_statement_verbatim: **Corollary 11.3 (Four-spoke descent and a stable descendant).** Let $`\mathcal D(H)`$ be tripartite, $`\nu(H)=h`$, $`\tau(H)=2h-1`$, and suppose $`H`$ is packing-edge-stable. Let $`U=\{a,b,c\}`$ be independent. Suppose the complete new triangle family obtained by restoring $`abc`$ consists exactly of $`abc`$ and its six pages at distinct apices $`p,q`$, with $`pq\notin E(H)`$, and suppose ``` math \nu(H+abc)=h+1,\qquad \tau(H+abc)=2h+2. ``` For any pair of compatible pages on different bases and at different apices, let $`A`$ be their four old spokes. Then ``` math \nu(H-A)=h-1,\qquad \tau(H-A)=2h-3. ``` A spoke is called active if it lies in an $`H`$-triangle. If at least five of the six spokes are active, such a pair can be chosen so that $`H-A`$ is packing-edge-stable. *Proof.* Exactness gives the boundary condition for $`U`$ and $`P=\{p,q\}`$: any outside vertex adjacent to two terminals would itself be an additional page apex. The two compatible pages append to any $`H-A`$ packing, giving $`\nu(H-A)\le h-1`$. The set $`A`$, together with the unused base edge, covers the entire individual new family and all old triangles destroyed by $`A`$. Hence $`\tau(H-A)\ge 2h-3`$. Aharoni now forces $`\nu(H-A)=h-1`$ and $`\tau(H-A)\in\{2h-3,2h-2\}`$. Theorem [11.1](#thm-boundary) excludes equality because $`H`$ is stable. With six active spokes, any four-spoke path has an active deleted spoke in every terminal row. With exactly five, make the deficient row the middle of the path: if $`ap`$ is inactive, use pages $`abp`$ and $`acq`$, so $`A=\{ap,bp,aq,cq\}`$ and $`aq,bp,cq`$ are active. The three nonempty rows supply three pairwise edge-disjoint lost triangles, by local uniqueness. Theorem [11.2](#thm-stability), with $`d=1`$, proves stability. $`\square`$ The five-active-spoke premise is explicit. No general reduction to that premise, and no iterative descent, is claimed: deleting $`A`$ damages the expensive family and supplies no replacement family. ## 12. Exact two-apex bowties

claims.available_statement_verbatim: **Lemma 12.1 (Nine-cycle page dichotomy).** Let $`L`$ have induced $`C_9`$ on $`W`$, independent outside part $`X`$, and arbitrary W-X spokes, and assume $`\nu(L)\le 4`$. Then either $`\tau(L)=\nu(L)`$, or its entire triangle family is a single full nine-wheel, with $`(\nu,\tau)=(4,5)`$. *Proof.* Represent the triangle family using its base edges and outside apices. Represent a triangle by ($`i,x`$), its cycle base and outside apex. Its intersection graph $`I`$ has clique columns $`i`$, and adjacent columns are joined only between equal apex labels. The neighborhood of any vertex is the disjoint union of its same-column clique and at most two singletons. Hence no neighborhood contains an induced $`P_3`$; this excludes odd antiholes of length at least seven, whose vertex neighborhoods contain $`P_3`$. Any induced cycle of $`I`$ of length at least five must visit all nine columns. Otherwise the used columns form a proper connected interval. An endpoint column cannot contain one cycle vertex (it has at most one neighbor in the sole adjacent used column). If it contains two, they are consecutive, their other cycle neighbors lie in the next column and are distinct, and the edge between those neighbors is a chord unless the cycle has length four. A clique column cannot contain three vertices of an induced cycle of length at least four. Thus $`C_5`$ and $`C_7`$ are absent. An induced $`C_9`$ uses one vertex per column and preserves its apex around the cycle, so it is a full nine-wheel. An odd hole of length at least eleven gives five independent vertices of $`I`$, hence a five-packing, contrary to $`\nu(L)\le 4`$. If a full wheel at $`x`$ exists together with a further page at $`y`$, remove that page’s base from $`C_9`$ and take a four-matching of the remaining eight-edge path. Its x-pages plus the y-page give a five-packing. Thus at $`\nu(L)\le 4`$ the full wheel must be the whole triangle family; it has $`(\nu,\tau)=(4,5)`$, since every edge meets at most two of its nine pages and a five-spoke cover exists. Without a wheel, the Strong Perfect Graph Theorem \[[4](#reference-4)\] applies (equivalently to the complement), so $`I`$ partitions into $`\alpha(I)=\nu(L)`$ cliques. Each clique has a common graph edge: a clique within one column has its base; a clique meeting two columns has exactly two vertices of the same apex and shares their joining spoke. There are no cliques spanning three columns. These common edges provide $`\tau(L)\le \nu(L)`$. This proves the dichotomy. $`\square`$

claims.available_statement_verbatim: **Theorem 12.2 (Mixed or shared-apex restoration).** Let $`G`$ be finite simple, $`T_1=vab`$ and $`T_2=vcd`$ edge-disjoint triangles sharing exactly $`v`$, and $`H=G-(E(T_1) \cup E(T_2))`$. Assume $`\mathcal D(H)`$ is 3-partite. For each $`i`$, the complete family of triangles in $`H+E(T_i)`$ but not in $`H`$ consists **exactly** of $`T_i`$ and its six pages at two distinct vertices $`P_i`$ adjacent to all three terminals. In particular there are no additional partial-apex pages. If $`P_1`$ intersects $`P_2`$, or if some $`G`$-triangle uses an edge of each $`T_i`$, then $`\tau(G)\le 2\nu(G)`$. The second alternative is equivalent to an $`H`$-edge between $`\{a,b\}`$ and $`\{c,d\}`$. This theorem does not settle vertex-disjoint restored triangles, disjoint-apex unmixed bowties, or arbitrary families of packing three. *Proof.* **Critical reduction and necessary full-family bookkeeping** Let $`h=\nu(H)`$. Appending $`T_1,T_2`$ gives $`\nu(G)\ge h+2`$; adding their six edges to an $`H`$-cover gives $`\tau(G)\le \tau(H)+6`$. Slack at least two settles immediately. The slack-zero branch is Section [6](#sec-exact). In a remaining counterexample, ``` math \begin{gathered} \tau(H)=2h-1, \nu(G)=h+2, \tau(G)=2h+5 \end{gathered} ``` **(12)** Theorem [7.2](#thm-essential) excludes essential edges of $`H`$. Each individual restoration must have actual cover increase three, since adding the other restored triangle’s three edges completes a cover of $`G`$. This uses actual tau of intermediate graphs, not just the cover number of a chosen new-family subcollection. The adjacent-apex lemma is independently proved as follows. For any terminal $`u`$, deleting its pair of spokes preserves $`\tau(H)`$, because those two spokes and the opposite base cover the individual new family at cost three. If $`pq`$ were present, delete triangle $`upq`$. Aharoni and cover loss force equality with $`h-1`$ $`K_4`$ blocks. For $`m=1`$ and cross matching $`pr,qs`$, the only lost internal triangle is $`vqs`$. At most one equality block contains $`qs`$. If such a block exists, omit it to get $`\nu(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{out}})\le 4`$. The exceptional pure wheel is impossible, because its outside apex would be adjacent to $`v,a,b`$ and thus be an extra first-family apex. Therefore $`\tau(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{out}})\le 4`$. A minimum $`J`$-cover can contain $`qs`$: choose $`qs`$ and its opposite edge in that block and opposite pairs in all others. It also covers $`vqs`$. Total cover at most $`2k+4=2h-2`$ contradicts slack one. claims.available_statement_verbatim: **Theorem 13.1 (Simultaneous compression).** Let $`H`$ be finite simple, $`\nu(H)=h`$, and $`\nu(H-e)=h`$ for every $`e`$ in $`E(H)`$. Add six absent edges forming two edge-disjoint triangles to obtain $`G`$; let $`S`$ be their endpoints, $`|S|\le 6`$. There exists a **subgraph**, not necessarily an induced subgraph, $`G'`$ containing all added edges. With $`H'`$ equal to $`G'`$ minus those six edges, ``` math \begin{gathered} \nu(G')=\nu(G), \tau(G')=\tau(G), \\ \nu(H')=\nu(H), \tau(H')=\tau(H), \\ |V(G')| \le 6h^2+3h+454 \end{gathered} ``` **(18)** $`H'`$ remains packing-edge-stable. If $`\mathcal D(H)`$ is 3-partite, so is $`\mathcal D(H')`$. More precisely, the nonisolated part of the old full triangle hypergraph is retained unchanged; deleted old graph edges are triangle-free hypergraph vertices. No claim of preserving the whole graph, induced structure, all covers, or all packings as literal subsets is made. *Proof.* For an edge $`ab`$, use an $`h`$-packing avoiding $`ab`$, available by stability. Every page $`abx`$ must meet this packing or could be appended. A packing triangle avoids $`ab`$ and therefore contains at most one of $`a,b`$; it can meet at most two distinct pages via its incident edges at that endpoint. Hence every $`H`$-edge lies in at most $`2h`$ triangles. Fix any maximum $`h`$-packing $`P`$. Every $`H`$-triangle meets one of its $`3h`$ edges. Counting incidences bounds the number of triangles by $`6h^2`$. Every such triangle has at least two vertices in $`V(P)`$, so the set A of all old-triangle vertices has size at most $`3h+6h^2`$. This includes $`h=0`$, when A is empty. Retain $`A \cup S`$. An outside vertex $`w`$ belongs to no old triangle. Any $`G`$-triangle through $`w`$ must use an added edge, which has both endpoints in $`S`$. Thus every edge incident to $`w`$ except an edge to $`S`$ lies in no $`G`$-triangle; remove all those edges. The remaining triangles through $`w`$ are exactly pages $`wxy`$ on added bases with $`x,y`$ in its exact S-neighborhood. Classify outside vertices by that neighborhood. There are at most $`2^6=64`$ types. Keep at most seven vertices per type, yielding ``` math \begin{gathered} |A|+|S|+7\cdot 64 \le 6h^2+3h+454 \end{gathered} ``` **(19)** All old triangles survive, so both old optimization parameters remain equal. For any retained old edge $`e`$, its old triangle incidence is unchanged; an $`h`$-packing avoiding $`e`$ still lies wholly within A. Hence old packing-edge stability is preserved, including retained triangle-free edges. Tripartiteness restricts directly. Any $`G`$-packing has at most six new triangles, since each consumes a distinct one of the six added edges. It therefore uses at most six distinct outside vertices. Within each truncated type injectively relabel the used outside vertices to retained representatives, fixing $`A \cup S`$. Neighborhood equality preserves triangles; injectivity preserves graph-edge disjointness. This sends every $`G`$-packing to a G’-packing of the same size; the reverse inequality follows from subgraph inclusion. For covers, take a minimum G’-cover $`C`$ and any truncated type with seven retained vertices $`W_N`$. Let $`D_N`$ be the added bases whose endpoints lie in its common neighborhood, $`|D_N|\le 6`$. If some $`xy`$ in $`D_N`$ were absent from $`C`$, each of the seven pages $`wxy`$ would require a distinct incident spoke $`wx`$ or $`wy`$ in $`C`$. Thus $`C`$ has at least seven edges incident with $`W_N`$. Replace all $`C`$ edges incident with $`W_N`$ by $`D_N`$. No other triangle loses coverage, because every triangle using a $`W_N`$ edge is one of its added-base pages. This yields a smaller cover, contradiction. Hence $`C`$ contains every $`D_N`$, so the same $`C`$ also covers all deleted vertices’ pages. Therefore $`\tau(G)\le \tau(G')`$, and subgraph monotonicity gives equality. $`\square`$ ## 14.
