original_row.source_exact_mathematical_interval: **Theorem 13.1 (Simultaneous compression).** Let $`H`$ be finite simple, $`\nu(H)=h`$, and $`\nu(H-e)=h`$ for every $`e`$ in $`E(H)`$. Add six absent edges forming two edge-disjoint triangles to obtain $`G`$; let $`S`$ be their endpoints, $`|S|\le 6`$. There exists a **subgraph**, not necessarily an induced subgraph, $`G'`$ containing all added edges. With $`H'`$ equal to $`G'`$ minus those six edges, ``` math \begin{gathered} \nu(G')=\nu(G), \tau(G')=\tau(G), \\ \nu(H')=\nu(H), \tau(H')=\tau(H), \\ |V(G')| \le 6h^2+3h+454 \end{gathered} ``` **(18)** $`H'`$ remains packing-edge-stable. If $`\mathcal D(H)`$ is 3-partite, so is $`\mathcal D(H')`$. More precisely, the nonisolated part of the old full triangle hypergraph is retained unchanged; deleted old graph edges are triangle-free hypergraph vertices. No claim of preserving the whole graph, induced structure, all covers, or all packings as literal subsets is made. *Proof.* For an edge $`ab`$, use an $`h`$-packing avoiding $`ab`$, available by stability. Every page $`abx`$ must meet this packing or could be appended. A packing triangle avoids $`ab`$ and therefore contains at most one of $`a,b`$; it can meet at most two distinct pages via its incident edges at that endpoint. Hence every $`H`$-edge lies in at most $`2h`$ triangles. Fix any maximum $`h`$-packing $`P`$. Every $`H`$-triangle meets one of its $`3h`$ edges. Counting incidences bounds the number of triangles by $`6h^2`$. Every such triangle has at least two vertices in $`V(P)`$, so the set A of all old-triangle vertices has size at most $`3h+6h^2`$. This includes $`h=0`$, when A is empty. Retain $`A \cup S`$. An outside vertex $`w`$ belongs to no old triangle. Any $`G`$-triangle through $`w`$ must use an added edge, which has both endpoints in $`S`$. Thus every edge incident to $`w`$ except an edge to $`S`$ lies in no $`G`$-triangle; remove all those edges. The remaining triangles through $`w`$ are exactly pages $`wxy`$ on added bases with $`x,y`$ in its exact S-neighborhood. Classify outside vertices by that neighborhood. There are at most $`2^6=64`$ types. Keep at most seven vertices per type, yielding ``` math \begin{gathered} |A|+|S|+7\cdot 64 \le 6h^2+3h+454 \end{gathered} ``` **(19)** All old triangles survive, so both old optimization parameters remain equal. For any retained old edge $`e`$, its old triangle incidence is unchanged; an $`h`$-packing avoiding $`e`$ still lies wholly within A. Hence old packing-edge stability is preserved, including retained triangle-free edges. Tripartiteness restricts directly. Any $`G`$-packing has at most six new triangles, since each consumes a distinct one of the six added edges. It therefore uses at most six distinct outside vertices. Within each truncated type injectively relabel the used outside vertices to retained representatives, fixing $`A \cup S`$. Neighborhood equality preserves triangles; injectivity preserves graph-edge disjointness. This sends every $`G`$-packing to a G’-packing of the same size; the reverse inequality follows from subgraph inclusion. For covers, take a minimum G’-cover $`C`$ and any truncated type with seven retained vertices $`W_N`$. Let $`D_N`$ be the added bases whose endpoints lie in its common neighborhood, $`|D_N|\le 6`$. If some $`xy`$ in $`D_N`$ were absent from $`C`$, each of the seven pages $`wxy`$ would require a distinct incident spoke $`wx`$ or $`wy`$ in $`C`$. Thus $`C`$ has at least seven edges incident with $`W_N`$. Replace all $`C`$ edges incident with $`W_N`$ by $`D_N`$. No other triangle loses coverage, because every triangle using a $`W_N`$ edge is one of its added-base pages. This yields a smaller cover, contradiction. Hence $`C`$ contains every $`D_N`$, so the same $`C`$ also covers all deleted vertices’ pages. Therefore $`\tau(G)\le \tau(G')`$, and subgraph monotonicity gives equality. $`\square`$ ## 14. A fixed-deficit density consequence The following is a derived corollary using the proof of Liu–Zeng \[[12](#reference-12)\], not a theorem quoted from their preprint. We give the modified estimates and the small-packing argument in detail, identifying the unchanged inputs. This section has not been formalized in Lean.

**Corollary 14.1 (Adaptation of Liu–Zeng).** For every fixed real $`c\lt 5/2`$ there exists $`N(c)`$ such that, for every integer $`n\ge N(c)`$ and every $`n`$-vertex graph $`G`$, $`e(G)\ge n^2/4-cn`$ implies $`\tau(G)\le2\nu(G)`$. **Imported approximation and elementary estimates.** Let $`\nu^*(G)`$ be the fractional triangle-packing optimum. We use $`\nu^*(G)-\nu(G)=o(n^2)`$, due to Haxell–Rödl \[[10](#reference-10)\]; alternatively Yuster’s Theorem 1.2 \[[15](#reference-15)\], with graph family $`\{K_3\}`$, suffices. Removing isolates leaves both optima unchanged. If the remaining order is large, its $`o(m^2)`$ error is bounded by the desired error in $`n^2`$; if bounded, its whole fractional optimum is a fixed constant. This handles Yuster’s convention excluding isolated vertices. Finite linear-programming duality identifies $`\nu^*`$ with the fractional edge-cover optimum. We also use Liu–Zeng Lemma 2.4: if $`S\subseteq E(J)`$ has at most one edge per triangle, $`C=E(J)\setminus S`$, and $`|C|\ge\beta n^2`$ for $`0\lt \beta\lt 1/2`$, then ``` math \tau(J)\le |C|-\beta^3n^2/36. ``` **(20)** This lemma has no density-deficit parameter. Their proof deletes a suitable cut complement, starting from $`\tau(J)\le|C|-e_C(A,B)+e_S(A)+e_S(B)`$ for disjoint $`A,B`$. Its independent-neighborhood partition gives savings at least $`\beta^3n^2/6`$, $`\beta^3n^2/36`$, or $`\beta n^2/24`$ according to the location of a large class of $`C`$-edges. Thus the common constant in [(20)](#eq-saving) remains unchanged here. *Proof of Corollary [14.1](#cor-density).* It suffices to treat $`0\le c\lt 5/2`$, since a negative $`c`$ has a stronger hypothesis than $`c=0`$. Put $`k=\nu(G)`$, $`t=\tau(G)`$ and take $`n`$ sufficiently large, as specified below. **Large packing: $`k\ge10^{-5}n^2`$.** This is Liu–Zeng’s Section 3, Case 1, unchanged: it uses no edge-count assumption or bound on $`c`$. Here is its quantitative core. If $`t>2k`$, choose the approximation error at most $`10^{-18}n^2`$ and write $`d=\nu^*(G)-t/2`$. The fractional-cover threshold argument in their equations (2)–(6), applied to weights in decreasing order, gives $`0\le d\lt 10^{-18}n^2`$. Partition the edges into $`L,M,F`$ according as their weights lie in $`[0,1/6)`$, $`[1/6,2/3)`$, $`[2/3,1]`$. The same argument gives ``` math |F|+|M|-t\le12d,\qquad |F|\le6d,\qquad |M|>10^{-5}n^2. ``` **(21)** For precision, the threshold inequalities are $`2f_i+f_{2t+1-i}\ge1`$ for $`1\le i\le t`$; summing bounds the weight after the first $`t`$ edges by $`2d`$, and clipping weights at $`1/2`$ bounds their total excess by $`d`$. These yield [(21)](#eq-large) exactly as in the cited case. A triangle in $`G-F`$ cannot have two $`L`$-edges, since their weights together with the third weight would sum to less than one. Apply [(20)](#eq-saving) with $`\beta=10^{-5}`$ to obtain ``` math t\le |F|+|M|-10^{-15}n^2/36 \lt t+(12\cdot10^{-18}-10^{-15}/36)n^2\lt t, ``` **(22)** a contradiction. All inputs to this case are independent of $`c`$. **A triangle-free decomposition.** For subsequent cases let $`H`$ be triangle-free and put $`\delta=n^2/4-e(H)`$, where $`0\le\delta\le10^{-4}n^2`$. Take a maximum-degree vertex of degree $`q`$, set $`V_1=N_H(v)`$ and $`V_2=V(H)\setminus V_1`$. Since $`V_1`$ is independent, $`e(H)+e_H(V_2)\le q(n-q)\le n^2/4`$. The number of missing cross pairs is at most $`2\delta`$, and each part differs from $`n/2`$ by at most $`\sqrt{2\delta}`$. Remove into $`A`$ every vertex missing more than $`n/5`$ neighbors in the other part; put $`B=V_1\setminus A`$, $`C=V_2\setminus A`$. Counting missing pairs twice gives ``` math |A|\le20\delta/n\le n/500,\quad |B|,|C|>9n/20. ``` **(23)** Every distinct pair in $`B`$ has more than $`n/20`$ common $`H`$-neighbors in $`C`$, and conversely. Hence $`B,C`$ are independent in $`H`$ and the missing $`B,C`$-pairs number at most $`2\delta`$. These are Liu–Zeng’s equations (7)–(13), with the deficit retained explicitly. **Intermediate packing: $`n^{2/3}\lt k\lt 10^{-5}n^2`$.** Remove a maximum packing $`\mathcal P`$ to form $`H`$. Then ``` math 0\le\delta\le cn+3k\le3n+3k\le10^{-4}n^2 ``` **(24)** eventually. The replacement of $`2n`$ by $`3n`$ is the first change to the source. Use the preceding decomposition. For $`x\in A`$, augment its $`H`$-neighbors in $`B`$ by the two vertices of each packing triangle $`xbb'`$; call this set $`L_x`$. Define $`R_x`$ analogously on $`C`$. There is no $`H`$-edge from $`L_x`$ to $`R_x`$. To see the exchange when such an edge $`bc`$ exists, if both $`xb,xc`$ are $`H`$-edges there is a triangle in $`H`$. If $`xbb'`$ is packed and $`xc`$ is in $`H`$, replace $`xbb'`$ by $`xbc`$ and $`bb'z`$, choosing a common $`H`$-neighbor $`z\in C`$ of $`b,b'`$ with $`z\ne c`$. The symmetric case is identical. If $`xbb'`$ and $`xcc'`$ are both packed, replace them by $`xbc,bb'z,cc'w`$, where $`z\in C\setminus\{c,c'\}`$ and $`w\in B\setminus\{b,b'\}`$ are appropriate common $`H`$-neighbors. The $`n/20`$ lower bounds permit these choices. The inserted triangles are edge-disjoint, and their new edges lie in $`H`$, so none meets a retained packing triangle. A packed triangle entirely in $`B`$ or $`C`$ similarly has a one-to-two exchange using two distinct common neighbors. Place each $`x\in A`$ on the side of the smaller of $`L_x,R_x`$. Their product counts missing $`B,C`$-pairs, so its smaller size is at most $`\sqrt{2\delta}`$. A packed triangle contributes one internal edge, plus two if all its vertices lie on one side. The extra contributions from triangles meeting $`A`$ once are already counted by the augmented sets. Let $`Q`$ be the wholly internal packed triangles meeting $`A`$ at least twice. They can be charged to distinct edges on $`A`$ outside $`H`$. Thus the internal $`H`$-edges on $`A`$ plus $`|Q|`$ number at most $`\binom{|A|}{2}`$, and these edges plus $`2|Q|`$ number at most $`|A|^2`$. Deleting all internal edges therefore gives $`t\le k+|A|\sqrt{2\delta}+|A|^2`$, hence ``` math t\le k+\frac{20\sqrt2}{n}\delta^{3/2}+\frac{400}{n^2}\delta^2. ``` **(25)** Using $`(a+b)^{3/2}\le\sqrt2(a^{3/2}+b^{3/2})`$, $`(a+b)^2\le2(a^2+b^2)`$, and [(24)](#eq-delta), we obtain ``` math \begin{aligned} \frac{t-k}{k}\le{}&120\sqrt3\,n^{-1/6} +120\sqrt{3\cdot10^{-5}}\\ &+7200n^{-2/3}+7200\cdot10^{-5}\lt 1 \end{aligned} ``` **(26)** eventually. The two constant terms sum to approximately $`0.729267069`$. For example $`n\ge10^{18}`$ suffices for this estimate and the elementary size conditions here. This proves $`t\le2k`$ in the intermediate case. **Small packing: $`k\le n^{2/3}`$, including equality.** Choose a spanning subgraph $`G'`$ with the fewest edges subject to $`e(G)-e(G')=k-k'`$, where $`k'=\nu(G')`$. Such a graph exists since $`G`$ qualifies, and ``` math \tau(G)\le k-k'+\tau(G'). ``` **(27)** Every edge of $`G'`$ has codegree at most $`2k'`$. Indeed, if $`uv`$ had more common neighbors, any packing in $`G'-uv`$ rules out at most two such neighbors per packed triangle. One further page $`uvw`$ extends it, forcing $`\nu(G'-uv)=k'-1`$. This would contradict the edge-minimal choice of $`G'`$ (Liu–Zeng Lemma 2.5). If $`k'=0`$, [(27)](#eq-restore) settles the claim. Otherwise remove a maximum packing from $`G'`$ to obtain a triangle-free $`H`$ with ``` math e(H)=e(G)-k-2k'\ge n^2/4-cn-3k\ge n^2/4-5n ``` **(28)** eventually. Thus the source’s constant $`5n`$ is unchanged for $`c\lt 5/2`$. The decomposition gives $`|A|\le100`$. Since $`n/20>2k'`$ eventually, its common-neighbor property and the codegree bound make $`B,C`$ independent even in $`G'`$. Place each $`x\in A`$ on the side with fewer $`H`$-neighbors. Their product is at most $`10n`$, since all pairs between these neighbor sets are missing cross pairs. The resulting parts $`X,Y`$ satisfy ``` math \begin{aligned} \bigl||X|-n/2\bigr|,\ \bigl||Y|-n/2\bigr|&\le\sqrt{10n}+100,\\ e_{G'}(X)+e_{G'}(Y)&\le4950+100\sqrt{10n}+3k'. \end{aligned} ``` **(29)** The first term $`4950`$ bounds edges inside $`A`$; at most $`100\sqrt{10n}`$ internal $`H`$-edges meet its complement, and all remaining edges removed in forming $`H`$ number $`3k'`$. Let $`S_1,S_2`$ be minimum vertex covers of the internal graphs on $`X,Y`$, and write $`s=|S_1|+|S_2|\le100`$; the parts of $`A`$ themselves cover these graphs. The following finite-witness fact is Liu–Zeng Lemma 2.6. A graph with a vertex cover of size $`a`$ has an induced subgraph on at most $`a^2+2a`$ vertices with the same minimum vertex-cover number: retain the cover and up to $`a+1`$ outside neighbors of each cover vertex. A cover of the retained graph of size at most $`a`$ extends to the whole graph. Otherwise a missed cover vertex with an omitted neighbor would have $`a+1`$ retained neighbors, a contradiction. The assertion also holds for $`a=0`$. Apply this to get witnesses $`T_1\subseteq X,T_2\subseteq Y`$ with their respective vertex-cover numbers $`|S_1|,|S_2|`$ and $`|T_1|+|T_2|\le s^2+2s\le10200`$. For $`y\in Y\setminus T_2`$, its nonneighbors in $`T_1`$, together with one endpoint of each edge among its neighbors in $`T_1`$, cover $`G'[T_1]`$. Summing and using the codegree bound gives at least ``` math |S_1|(|Y|-|T_2|)-2k'e_{G'}(T_1) ``` **(30)** missing pairs in $`T_1\times(Y\setminus T_2)`$. The symmetric count lies in $`(X\setminus T_1)\times T_2`$, a disjoint set of pairs. Use ``` math \begin{aligned} e_{G'}(T_1)+e_{G'}(T_2)&\le\binom{10200}{2}=52,014,900,\\ |S_1||T_2|+|S_2||T_1|&\le1,020,000. \end{aligned} ``` **(31)** Subtracting both missing-pair counts from $`|X||Y|\le n^2/4`$ and adding the internal edges from [(29)](#eq-small-partition) yields ``` math e(G')\le\frac{n^2}{4}-\frac{s}{2}n +200\sqrt{10n}+1,034,950+104,029,803k'. ``` **(32)** The constant terms are $`100s+1,020,000+4950\le1,034,950`$; the coefficient of $`k'`$ is $`2\cdot52,014,900+3`$. Compare with $`e(G')\ge n^2/4-cn-k+k'`$ and use $`k'\le k\le n^{2/3}`$ to obtain ``` math \left(\frac{s}{2}-c\right)n \le104,029,803n^{2/3}+200\sqrt{10n}+1,034,950. ``` **(33)** For $`n\ge1`$ the right side is less than $`106,000,000n^{2/3}`$. Put $`\varepsilon=5/2-c>0`$. If $`s\ge5`$, [(33)](#eq-key) is impossible for $`n>(106,000,000/\varepsilon)^3`$. Hence $`s\le4`$. Deleting $`S_1\cup S_2`$ makes $`G'`$ bipartite. Corollary [4.3](#cor-oct) gives $`\tau(G')\le2k'`$, and [(27)](#eq-restore) gives $`\tau(G)\le k+k'\le2k`$. One sufficient $`N(c)`$ is the maximum of $`10^{18}`$, the threshold for the imported fractional approximation with error $`10^{-18}n^2`$, and an integer strictly exceeding $`(106,000,000/(5/2-c))^3`$. For $`c\lt 0`$ use $`N(0)`$. No numerical threshold for the deep approximation is asserted. The strict positivity of $`5/2-c`$ is essential to the last step: this proof establishes neither the endpoint $`c=5/2`$ nor a threshold uniform as $`c`$ approaches it. This completes the adaptation. $`\square`$ ## 15. Verification, evidence and open questions ### 15.1 Exact formal boundary The archived projects use Lean 4.33.1 and pinned Mathlib dependencies. All graph triangles are actual three-cliques and all extremal values are actual finite packing maxima and cover minima. The following list maps the numbered statements to their completed declarations; identifiers are intentionally separated from prose to remain readable. Theorem [2.1](#thm-main) and Corollary [4.3](#cor-oct).
`Tuza.triangle_deletion` `Tuza.oct_four`, with explicit AharoniInput and HNSInput. Theorem [6.1](#thm-exact).
`Tuza.two_triangle_exact_equality`, with HNSInput. Theorem [7.2](#thm-essential).
`Tuza.two_triangle_essential_edge_restoration` `Tuza.two_triangle_essential_family_saving`, with AharoniInput and HNSInput. Theorem [11.1](#thm-boundary).
`Tuza.closed_boundary_equality_deletion` `Tuza.closed_boundary_packing_loss`. Inputs: AharoniInput, HNSInput and `BipartiteKonigInput (Finset V)`. Theorem [11.2](#thm-stability).
`Tuza.closed_boundary_stability`, with AharoniInput and HNSInput. AharoniInput states the tripartite full-triangle bound. HNSInput supplies edge-disjoint graphical $`K_4`$s and packages both published home-base extraction and the graphical loose-cycle conversion in Lemma [3.2](#lem-k4). Those inputs, including that conversion, remain assumed in Lean. Classical bipartite König matching–cover equality \[[11](#reference-11)\] is an explicit input to the boundary integrality theorem; the triangle-to-pair conversion, injectivity, matching compatibility and cover conversion are proved. Hall’s matching theorem \[[6](#reference-6)\] is used through the pinned formal library in the essential-edge proof. The transitive axiom reports contain only `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`. They do not discharge explicit theorem parameters. The archived publication verification independently rebuilt the full public project from published sources: 18 modules, 17 serial kernel replays, and 152 declaration/axiom reports, using nine pinned compiled dependencies. This was not a cold Mathlib rebuild or an external independent prover check. The flat, star-core, mixed/shared-apex bowtie and compression results, the separate four-spoke application, and the density consequence have audited ordinary proofs without corresponding full Lean formalization. The formal equality-bowtie case in Theorem [6.1](#thm-exact) is distinct from Theorem [12.2](#thm-bowtie). ### 15.2 Negative evidence and finite certificates A wheel with five rim vertices and one hub has $`(\nu,\tau)=(2,3)`$ and a tripartite full triangle hypergraph. Deleting its hub leaves no triangles. It refutes the proposed inequality $`\tau(H)\le \nu(H)+\nu(H-U)`$ for independent $`U`$. It does not refute restoration. A central $`K_4`$ with one, two, or three fresh $`K_4`$ leaves on distinct edges of a central star has parameters $`(r+1,2r+1)`$ and no packing-essential edge. These examples refute an overly small list of possible defective cores. The scoped restoration proofs for those three cores are retained as supporting TUZA-02 material. The difference between individual and full incident families is substantive. Take $`K_5`$ on 0,1,2,3,4 and add edges 15 and 35, with restored triangles 012 and 034. The remainder and restored graph have parameters $`(1,1)`$ and $`(3,4)`$. The full incident families have cover number three, but the individual restoration families each have cover number one. An enlarged-family formulation is therefore false. The archived verification replay regenerated all graph triangles and checked 35 recurrence certificates, the three star examples by a separate subset-enumeration implementation, their surviving packings after every single-edge deletion, and the family-definition example. An additional independent script checked 70 finite local packing/cover configurations used in the bowtie case proofs. These are named-certificate checks, not an exhaustive search over arbitrary graphs; the general theorems rest on their ordinary proofs. ### 15.3 Scope, originality and remaining questions **Unrestricted two-triangle restoration, OCT-five and the fixed-$`c\lt 3`$ density extension remain unproved.** The density proof also establishes neither its endpoint $`c=5/2`$ nor a threshold uniform near that endpoint. General stable, nonflat, slack-one remainders remain outside the restoration theorems. Exact bowties with disjoint apices and no mixed triangle, and arbitrary individual families of packing three, are not settled here. The compression theorem does not bound $`h`$ or reduce unrestricted restoration to one finite computation. Existing linear-size decision kernels for individual edge-triangle packing and covering \[[13](#reference-13)\] preclude an improved-kernel-size claim for this quadratic simultaneous-preservation argument. Fractional stability results \[[8](#reference-8)\] have a fractional-cover hypothesis and cannot be invoked from integer slack one. This is AI-assisted research under the neutral attribution AI Math Experiments. Internal independent reconstruction and editorial review are not external specialist peer review. Targeted literature comparisons found no exact predecessor for selected statements, but historical originality and priority are not established. The exact-equality two-triangle extension originated in a follow-up preceding TUZA-02; the three campaigns retain separate provenance. The canonical paper integrates their accepted proofs without changing the archived statements or verification evidence.

All graph triangles are actual three-cliques and all extremal values are actual finite packing maxima and cover minima. The following list maps the numbered statements to their completed declarations; identifiers are intentionally separated from prose to remain readable. Theorem [2.1](#thm-main) and Corollary [4.3](#cor-oct).
`Tuza.triangle_deletion` `Tuza.oct_four`, with explicit AharoniInput and HNSInput. Theorem [6.1](#thm-exact).
`Tuza.two_triangle_exact_equality`, with HNSInput. Theorem [7.2](#thm-essential).
`Tuza.two_triangle_essential_edge_restoration` `Tuza.two_triangle_essential_family_saving`, with AharoniInput and HNSInput. Theorem [11.1](#thm-boundary).
`Tuza.closed_boundary_equality_deletion` `Tuza.closed_boundary_packing_loss`. Inputs: AharoniInput, HNSInput and `BipartiteKonigInput (Finset V)`. Theorem [11.2](#thm-stability).

General stable, nonflat, slack-one remainders remain outside the restoration theorems. Exact bowties with disjoint apices and no mixed triangle, and arbitrary individual families of packing three, are not settled here. The compression theorem does not bound $`h`$ or reduce unrestricted restoration to one finite computation. Existing linear-size decision kernels for individual edge-triangle packing and covering \[[13](#reference-13)\] preclude an improved-kernel-size claim for this quadratic simultaneous-preservation argument. Fractional stability results \[[8](#reference-8)\] have a fractional-cover hypothesis and cannot be invoked from integer slack one. This is AI-assisted research under the neutral attribution AI Math Experiments. Internal independent reconstruction and editorial review are not external specialist peer review. Targeted literature comparisons found no exact predecessor for selected statements, but historical originality and priority are not established. The exact-equality two-triangle extension originated in a follow-up preceding TUZA-02; the three campaigns retain separate provenance. The canonical paper integrates their accepted proofs without changing the archived statements or verification evidence.

claims.available_statement_verbatim:
**Theorem 1 (Main theorem).** Every finite simple 5-degenerate graph $G$ satisfies

$$\tau(G)\le2\nu(G).$$

Equality holds if and only if every nonempty shared-edge triangle component has edge support $K_4$ or $K_5$.

A graph is **5-degenerate** if every nonempty vertex-induced subgraph has a vertex of degree at most five in that subgraph. Equivalently, every nonempty subgraph has such a vertex: deleting edges cannot increase degrees. This is a degeneracy condition, with no bound on original maximum degree. It does not imply maximum average degree less than seven. The theorem includes the empty graph and every triangle-free graph: both parameters vanish and the component condition is vacuous.

Two triangles are adjacent if they share an **edge**. Their connected components under chains of this adjacency are the *triangle components*. The edge support of a component is the union of its triangle edges. This differs from ordinary graph connectedness: distinct triangle components may share vertices, and edges lying in no triangle affect neither parameter. All triangle families used below are the full families of their graphs unless a subfamily is expressly named. A string $abc$ denotes the triangle on distinct vertices $a,b,c$, and $ab$ its graph edge. We write $N(v)$ and $N[v]$ for open and closed neighborhoods, $d(v)$ for degree, and $G[N(v)]$ for a vertex link.

**Equivalent block formulation.** The component condition is equivalent to the existence of a finite family of pairwise edge-disjoint actual $K_4$ and $K_5$ subgraphs containing every graph triangle. To prove this, component supports give such a family directly. Conversely, assign each triangle to a containing block. Triangles in different blocks cannot share an edge, by edge disjointness. Within $K_4$ or $K_5$ its triangles are connected by shared edges: two triangles sharing only a vertex are joined by a triangle using that vertex and one other vertex from each. Every block edge belongs to a triangle. Thus a triangle component consists exactly of one block's full triangle family, and its literal edge support is that clique. This argument checks the literal component condition rather than assuming it from a supplied decomposition. Since packing and covering numbers add over edge-disjoint triangle supports, the elementary parameters in Lemma 2 prove the equality converse for arbitrary graphs.

The proof's starting framework is due to Puleo [2, Definition 2.1 and Lemma 2.2]. His robustness and local low-degree results [2, Lemmas 2.6--2.7 and Propositions 5.1--5.2] are predecessors of Sections 3--6; the four/eight reducing pair in Section 6.2 is the witness in his Proposition 5.2, Case 1. Botler, Fernandes and Gutiérrez [3, Lemma 3.3] provide the direct predecessor of Proposition 8 for irreducible robust graphs. The extra requirement here is that balanced reductions need not contradict a minimal failure of the **combined** statement. We therefore derive exact residual equality, classify its clique supports, and prove compatibility and strict improvements at each balanced case. These extensions, especially arbitrary outside-page compatibility and the thirteen-versus-fourteen cover saving, remain explicit below. Appendix A gives the shorter credited inequality deduction, for which balanced reductions suffice.

Cui, Haxell and Ma [4, Theorem 1.2 and Section 2] characterize planar equality using edge-disjoint $K_4$ copies containing every triangle, with triangle-free background edges allowed. Theorem 1 recovers their known case because planar graphs are 5-degenerate and contain no $K_5$. Their theorem is not claimed as a new consequence in historical terms. Puleo's main sparsity theorem assumes maximum average degree less than seven. This class and the class of all five-degenerate graphs are incomparable. The graph $K_7$ has maximum average degree six but is not five-degenerate. In the other direction, start with $K_5$ and add five pairwise nonadjacent vertices, each joined to every original clique vertex. There are ten vertices and $10+25=35$ edges, so the average degree is seven and the maximum average degree is at least seven. Removing the five new degree-five vertices first and then the clique gives a five-degeneracy ordering. Thus this graph is outside Puleo's hypothesis. We use his local framework rather than a containment between these classes. Botler--Fernandes--Gutiérrez prove a treewidth theorem; their local lemma is the antecedent used here, not an invented degeneracy version of their main result.

**Recent context.** Gupta [5, Theorem 1.3], arXiv:2608.06538v1 (6 August 2026), proves Tuza's inequality for graphs of maximum degree at most seven. His Question 12.3 asks for the equality cases in that class. Theorem 1 supplies the equality classification on its intersection with the five-degenerate class. It does not answer the whole question: in particular, a nonempty seven-regular graph is not five-degenerate. Gupta's maximum-degree theorem is not used to prove Theorem 1.

Liu and Zeng [6, Theorem 1.3], arXiv:2610.15539v1 (11 October 2026), establish the inequality for every fixed $c<2$ and sufficiently large $n$ under $e(G)\ge n^2/4-cn$. This is an edge-count condition, distinct from the degeneracy assumption here; no density-class conclusion is inferred from Theorem 1. The [separate triangle-restoration report](../tuza-triangle-restoration/main.md) [8] retains its own statements and verification boundary.

### Reading the proof

Sections 1--5 establish clique compatibility, tight criticality, robustness, and the two possible degree-five links. Sections 6--7 prove all degree-five adjacency, neighbor and overlap restrictions for a minimal combined obstruction. Section 8 applies degeneracy a second time, reconstructs the final core, and excludes arbitrary outside attachments. Section 9 closes the induction. Section 10 gives a concise verification account. Appendix A contains the short inequality proof, Appendix B the small-link proof organization used in Lean, and Appendix C the detailed declaration coverage and verification provenance. Every ordinary proof needed for Theorem 1 is contained here.

For a local vertex set $W$, an **external page** is a triangle with base edge in $W$ and apex outside the specified core; its apex-to-base edges are its spokes. Different pages may share an apex. A *surviving footprint* means only edges actually remaining in the explicitly named residual graph. No bound is imposed on outside vertices or edges. Partial spoke deletion at a closed link component removes just its spokes, retaining all other neighbors; closure ensures that no unlisted hub triangle crosses to another link component.

A *surviving footprint* means only edges actually remaining in the explicitly named residual graph. No bound is imposed on outside vertices or edges. Partial spoke deletion at a closed link component removes just its spokes, retaining all other neighbors; closure ensures that no unlisted hub triangle crosses to another link component.

**Lemma 2 (Clique parameters and compatibility).** The graphs $K_4$ and $K_5$ have packing/covering numbers (1,2) and (2,4). A maximum $K_4$ packing avoids a star; a maximum $K_5$ packing avoids any two prescribed edges. Every edge belongs to some minimum cover.

*Proof.*

$K_4$ has $(\nu,\tau)=(1,2)$. $K_5$ has $(\nu,\tau)=(2,4)$: two edge-disjoint triangles exist; three edge-disjoint triangles would use nine edges and leave one edge, impossible because every degree in a union of edge-disjoint triangles is even whereas removing one edge from $K_5$ creates two odd degrees. Each edge of $K_5$ meets three of its ten triangles, so three cover edges cannot cover them all; four edges inside a vertex bipartition of sizes two and three do cover all triangles.

A $K_4$ maximum packing can avoid any star of forbidden edges by choosing the face opposite the star center. A $K_5$ maximum packing can avoid any two edges. Up to relabeling, for forbidden adjacent edges 12,13 choose 145,234; for forbidden disjoint edges 12,34 choose 135,245. Each displayed pair is edge-disjoint. Zero or one forbidden edge follows by enlarging the forbidden set.

In either block there is a minimum cover containing any specified edge. In $K_4$ take it and its opposite edge. In $K_5$ take the four edges inside a $2+3$ vertex partition whose two-vertex class is that edge's endpoints. Independent choices combine across triangle components, whose edge supports are disjoint.

We also use the elementary intersecting-triangle lemma: a pairwise edge-intersecting triangle family has a two-edge cover; if it has no common edge, all its triangles are faces of a single $K_4$. Indeed, two distinct triangles can be written $abc$,$abd$. A triangle avoiding $ab$ must share another edge with each, hence is $acd$ or $bcd$. Once such a triangle is present, every further triangle lies among those four faces. The pair $ab$,$cd$ covers the family. Families with a common edge, or a single triangle, are immediate.

**Lemma 2A (Block-packing compatibility).** Let $K$ be a subgraph of $G$ whose full triangle components have $K_4$ or $K_5$ supports, and let $P$ be a family of $k$ pairwise edge-disjoint $G$-triangles. For each component block $B$, let $D_B=E(B)\cap\bigcup_{T\in P}E(T)$. Suppose $D_B$ is contained in a star when $B$ is $K_4$, and $|D_B|\le2$ when $B$ is $K_5$. Then $\nu(G)\ge\nu(K)+k$.

*Proof.* By Lemma 2 choose a maximum packing in each block avoiding $D_B$. The blocks have disjoint edge supports, so these packings combine into a packing of size $\nu(K)$. It is edge-disjoint from every member of $P$ by the definition of $D_B$. Appending $P$ proves the bound.

**Two-page use and its bound.** If a terminal set $S$ is independent in $K$, each clique block meets $S$ in at most one vertex. For two pages with bases in $S$, each page contributes at most one surviving edge to a block: a block containing both spokes would contain both base endpoints. The union of the surviving spokes is therefore a star with at most two edges, satisfying both cases of Lemma 2A. A star alone is not sufficient for a $K_5$ block. In every application below we state the bound on the entire surviving footprint, including any contribution from local packed triangles.

claims.available_statement_verbatim:
**Lemma 3 (Tight criticality).** An edge-minimal failure of the combined statement in a subgraph-closed class, after removing isolated vertices, has one nonempty triangle component, no triangle-free edges, and $\tau(G)=2\nu(G)$. Every edge deletion preserves $\nu$ and decreases $\tau$ by one.

*Proof.*

Call $S$ the assertion that Tuza's inequality holds and equality implies the $K_4$/$K_5$ component condition. The converse has already been proved in the introduction. A failure therefore means either $\tau(G)>2\nu(G)$, or $\tau(G)=2\nu(G)$ with an unclassified component. Let $C$ be any class closed under taking subgraphs, and suppose $G$ is a failure of $S$ in $C$ with as few edges as possible. Discard isolated vertices. Then every proper edge-subgraph satisfies $S$.

There are no triangle-free edges: deleting one preserves the triangle family and the failure. There is only one nonempty triangle component. Indeed, the support subgraph of a triangle component has exactly that component as its full triangle family: any triangle using its support edges shares an edge with a component member, so belongs to the same shared-edge component. If there were several nonempty components, each support subgraph would have fewer edges and minimality would apply $S$ to it. Summing their inequalities, equality of the sum forces equality and the block classification in every component. Thus $G$ has connected nonempty triangle support.

Write $h=\nu(G)$. A failure of $S$ has $\tau(G)\ge 2h$. If $\nu(G-f)=h-1$ for an edge $f$, induction gives $\tau(G)\le \tau(G-f)+1\le 2h-1$, impossible. Hence every edge deletion preserves $\nu$.

If $\tau(G-f)=2h$ for $f=xy$, then $G-f$ has only $K_4$/$K_5$ triangle components. Choose a triangle $xyw$ of $G$. The wedge edges $xw$,$yw$ cannot lie in the same residual clique block, since $xy$ is absent. Each residual block contains at most one of $xw,yw$ because $xy$ is absent. Thus its forbidden footprint is a star of size at most one. Lemma 2A, with $P=\{xyw\}$, gives $h+1$ triangles, contradiction. Therefore $\tau(G-f)\le 2h-1$ for every edge $f$. Cover deletion changes $\tau$ by at most one, so


$$
\tau(G)=2h; \nu(G-f)=h; \tau(G-f)=2h-1 \quad\text{for every edge }f
$$


Thus every minimal $S$-obstruction in a hereditary class is tight-critical. This argument proves the reduction; it does not presume global Tuza.

**Lemma 3A (Balanced-reduction accounting).** Let $G$ be the edge-minimal combined obstruction of Lemma 3, write $h=\nu(G)$, and let $K$ be a proper subgraph in the same subgraph-closed class. Suppose that $P$ consists of $r$ pairwise edge-disjoint $G$-triangles, no edge used by $P$ lies in the triangle support of $K$, and $X\subseteq E(G)$ meets every $G$-triangle not belonging to the full triangle family of $K$. If $|X|\le2r$, then

$$\nu(K)=h-r,\qquad \tau(K)=2\nu(K),\qquad |X|=2r,$$

and $K$ has the component-block classification. In particular, $|X|<2r$ is impossible.

*Proof.* The support condition lets every $K$-packing append $P$, so $\nu(K)+r\le h$. A minimum $K$-cover together with $X$ covers every $G$-triangle by the stated lost-triangle condition. Minimality supplies both the inequality and the equality conclusion for $K$. Consequently

$$2h=\tau(G)\le\tau(K)+|X|\le2\nu(K)+2r\le2h.$$

Every inequality is an equality. This gives the displayed accounting and licenses the residual component classification. No residual equality is assumed before this chain is proved.

A useful instance is the reducible-set framework of Puleo [2, Definition 2.1 and Lemma 2.2]. For a nonempty vertex set $U$, a packing $P$ of size $r$, and an edge set $X$ hitting every triangle incident with $U$ and containing every $P$-edge with neither end in $U$, put $K=(G-X)-U$. The packing and lost-triangle hypotheses of Lemma 3A then follow directly. The partial-spoke deletions below use the same hypotheses, checked on their displayed witnesses.

**Lemma 4 (Triangle codegree).** Every edge of a minimal combined obstruction belongs to at least two triangles.

*Proof.*

Suppose $uv$ belongs only to $uvw$. Delete $uw$,$vw$ to get $K$. The edge $uv$ is triangle-free in $K$, so every $K$-packing can be appended by $uvw$. A $K$-cover plus $uw$,$vw$ covers $G$. Hence $\nu(K)=h-1$, $\tau(K)=2h-2$ and $K$ has the block classification. Each block meets $U_0=\{u,v,w\}$ at most once: $uw$,$vw$ are absent, and $uv$ is triangle-free in $K$.

Let $F$ be the full family of triangles lost in this deletion. They all contain $w$. If $F$ is intersecting, the preceding lemma says that $F$ has a common edge or is contained in $K_4$ faces. In the latter case, since $uvw$ belongs to $F$ and all $F$-triangles contain $w$, absence of a common edge forces $wuv$,$wux$,$wvx$ for a fourth vertex $x$. Their edges force the triangle $uvx$, contradicting uniqueness of $uvw$. Thus $F$ has a one-edge cover, giving $\tau(G)\le \tau(K)+1<2h$.

If $F$ is not intersecting, take two disjoint members. Each block meets $U_0$ in at most one vertex. The two selected triangles therefore have a star footprint there, with each triangle contributing at most one surviving edge. Its size is at most two, including for $K_5$. Lemma 2A gives $h+1$ triangles, contradiction. Therefore every $G$-edge has triangle codegree at least two. Equivalently every vertex in every link $G[N(v)]$ has degree at least two.

claims.available_statement_verbatim:
**Lemma 5 (Robustness).** Every connected component of every vertex link in a minimal combined obstruction has at least five vertices; in particular the obstruction $G$ has minimum degree at least five.

*Proof.*

Let $C_0$ be a connected component of the link at $v$. In the following cases, deleting $v$ means deleting just the spokes into $C_0$; other neighbors of $v$ remain. There is no triangle through a deleted spoke with its third vertex outside $C_0$, because that would join link components. All listed covers therefore account for every lost triangle. External rim pages have apex outside $C_0\cup \{v\}$.

### 4.1 Link component $K_3$

Write $C_0=abc$. Delete its three $v$-spokes and $ab$. The triangle $vab$ appends to any residual $K$-packing, and $\{ab,vc\}$ is a cover increment, so $K$ has equality blocks and $\nu(K)=h-1$.

An external $abx$ combines with $vbc$. Their edges present in $K$ are $bc$,$ax$,$bx$. Since $ab$ is deleted, no block contains both $a$ and $b$; the only possible two-edge overlap is $bc$,$bx$, a star at $b$. The whole footprint in a block is thus a star of size at most two; Lemma 2A yields $h+1$ triangles, contradiction. By symmetry no rim edge of $abc$ has an external triangle. Thus the $K_4$ on $v$,$a$,$b$,$c$ is an isolated triangle component. Connectedness makes it the whole triangle support, which satisfies $S$, contradiction.

### 4.2 Link component $K_4$

Write $C_0=abcd$. Delete its $v$-spokes and $ab$,$cd$. The packing $vab$,$vcd$ appends, and $\{ab,cd,va,vb\}$ is a four-edge cover increment. Hence $\nu(K)=h-2$ and $K$ has equality blocks.

An external $abx$ combines with $vac$,$vbd$. Its old forbidden edges are $ac$,$bd$,$ax$,$bx$. Because $ab$ is absent, a block sees at most two of these edges, necessarily adjacent at $a$ or $b$. The whole footprint is a star with at most two edges, so Lemma 2A gives $h+1$ triangles. Varying the perfect matching $ab$,$cd$ excludes external triangles on every rim edge. The $K_5$ on $v$,$a$,$b$,$c$,$d$ is therefore an isolated triangle component, again impossible.

### 4.3 Diamond link component

Write $C_0=K_4-ab$ on $a$,$b$,$c$,$d$. Delete its $v$-spokes and $ac$,$bd$. Use packing $vac$,$vbd$ and cover increment $\{ac,bd,vc,vd\}$; equality gives $\nu(K)=h-2$ and blocks.

An external $acx$ combines with $vad$,$vbc$. Its old forbidden edges are $ad$,$bc$,$ax$,$cx$. Since $ac$ is absent in $K$, a block sees at most two of these, with the only possible pairs $ad$,$ax$ or $bc$,$cx$. Each full block footprint is a star of size at most two; Lemma 2A contradicts maximality. By symmetry, including use of the other matching $ad$,$bc$, no external triangle uses $ac$,$ad$,$bc$,$bd$. Returning to $K$ above, a $K$-cover plus $\{vc,vd,cd\}$ covers $G$: $vc$,$vd$ cover all $v$-triangles, and the only other lost triangles are $acd$,$bcd$, hit by $cd$. This gives $2h-1$ cover edges, contradiction.

### 4.4 Four-cycle link component

Let $C_0$ be a connected component of the link at $v$. In the following cases, deleting $v$ means deleting just the spokes into $C_0$; other neighbors of $v$ remain. There is no triangle through a deleted spoke with its third vertex outside $C_0$, because that would join link components. All listed covers therefore account for every lost triangle. External rim pages have apex outside $C_0\cup \{v\}$.

### 4.1 Link component $K_3$

Write $C_0=abc$. Delete its three $v$-spokes and $ab$. The triangle $vab$ appends to any residual $K$-packing, and $\{ab,vc\}$ is a cover increment, so $K$ has equality blocks and $\nu(K)=h-1$.

An external $abx$ combines with $vbc$. Their edges present in $K$ are $bc$,$ax$,$bx$. Since $ab$ is deleted, no block contains both $a$ and $b$; the only possible two-edge overlap is $bc$,$bx$, a star at $b$. The whole footprint in a block is thus a star of size at most two; Lemma 2A yields $h+1$ triangles, contradiction. By symmetry no rim edge of $abc$ has an external triangle. Thus the $K_4$ on $v$,$a$,$b$,$c$ is an isolated triangle component. Connectedness makes it the whole triangle support, which satisfies $S$, contradiction.

### 4.2 Link component $K_4$

Write $C_0=abcd$. Delete its $v$-spokes and $ab$,$cd$. The packing $vab$,$vcd$ appends, and $\{ab,cd,va,vb\}$ is a four-edge cover increment. Hence $\nu(K)=h-2$ and $K$ has equality blocks.

An external $abx$ combines with $vac$,$vbd$. Its old forbidden edges are $ac$,$bd$,$ax$,$bx$. Because $ab$ is absent, a block sees at most two of these edges, necessarily adjacent at $a$ or $b$. The whole footprint is a star with at most two edges, so Lemma 2A gives $h+1$ triangles. Varying the perfect matching $ab$,$cd$ excludes external triangles on every rim edge. The $K_5$ on $v$,$a$,$b$,$c$,$d$ is therefore an isolated triangle component, again impossible.

### 4.3 Diamond link component

Write $C_0=K_4-ab$ on $a$,$b$,$c$,$d$. Delete its $v$-spokes and $ac$,$bd$. Use packing $vac$,$vbd$ and cover increment $\{ac,bd,vc,vd\}$; equality gives $\nu(K)=h-2$ and blocks.

Since $ac$ is absent in $K$, a block sees at most two of these, with the only possible pairs $ad$,$ax$ or $bc$,$cx$. Each full block footprint is a star of size at most two; Lemma 2A contradicts maximality. By symmetry, including use of the other matching $ad$,$bc$, no external triangle uses $ac$,$ad$,$bc$,$bd$. Choose a minimum $K$-cover containing $bc$, and add only $ab$,$cd$,$da$. It covers $G$ with $2h-1$ edges, contradiction.

**Lemma 6 (Degree-five links).** The link of every degree-five vertex in a minimal combined obstruction is $K_5$ or $K_5$ minus one edge.

*Proof.*

Robustness forces the link of a degree-five vertex to be connected: its components each have at least five vertices, and its total order is five. We first exclude its 3-colorable possibilities, and then treat the non-3-colorable case.

Suppose a link component $L$ has five vertices, minimum degree at least two, and is 3-colorable. Its complement has maximum degree at most two. A 3-coloring gives either a size-three color class (a triangle in the complement) or two size-two classes (a matching of size two). There are eleven unlabeled graphs on five vertices of maximum degree at most two: $5I$, $K_2+3I$, $2K_2+I$, $P_3+2I$, $P_3+K_2$, $P_4+I$, $P_5$, $C_3+2I$, $C_3+K_2$, $C_4+I$, and $C_5$. Here $I=K_1$ and $+$ denotes disjoint union. The first, second, and fourth entries have non-3-colorable complements; the other eight are the possible complements here. Thus the possible complements are exactly


$$
2K_2+I, P_3+K_2, P_4+I, P_5, C_3+K_2, C_3+2I, C_4+I, C_5
$$


For a matching $M$ and vertex set $Q$ with $L-Q$ a subgraph of $M$, delete the local $v$-spokes and $M$. The $|M|$ triangles at $v$ on $M$ append to every residual packing, while $M$ plus the $v$-spokes to $Q$ is a cover increment. If $|Q|<|M|$ this is strict; if equality holds, the residual has $K_4$/$K_5$ blocks and packing $h-|M|$.

### 5.1 Four dense types

In each dense case $|M|=|Q|=2$. The listed three triangles are mutually edge-disjoint. Their edges present in the residual are listed as their surviving footprint. The missing and deleted edges restrict a block's intersection as shown, so every whole block footprint is a star with at most two edges. Lemma 2A appends all three triangles, contradiction.

**Dense case 1.** Let $L$ be $K_{2,3}$ with sides $\{p,q\}$,$\{b,c,x\}$, plus $bc$. Take $M=\{bc,px\}$ and $Q=\{p,q\}$. The three triangles are $pbc$; $vqb$; $vpx$; their surviving footprint is $\{pb,pc,qb\}$. Possible two-edge overlap in a block: none: $bc$ deleted and $pq$ absent.

**Dense case 2.** Let $L$ be $K_5$ minus $ab$,$bc$,$cd$; fifth vertex $e$. Take $M=\{bd,ce\}$ and $Q=\{a,e\}$. The three triangles are $ace$; $vad$; $vbe$; their surviving footprint is $\{ac,ae,ad,be\}$. Possible two-edge overlap in a block: only $ae$,$ad$.

**Dense case 3.** Let $L$ be $K_5$ minus $ab$,$bc$,$cd$,$de$. Take $M=\{ac,bd\}$ and $Q=\{a,e\}$. The three triangles are $ace$; $vad$; $vbe$; their surviving footprint is $\{ae,ce,ad,be\}$. Possible two-edge overlap in a block: none.

**Dense case 4.** Let $L$ be $K_{2,3}$ with sides $\{p,q\}$,$\{a,b,c\}$, plus $pq$. Take $M=\{ap,bq\}$ and $Q=\{p,q\}$. The three triangles are $apq$; $vbp$; $vcq$; their surviving footprint is $\{aq,pq,bp,cq\}$. Possible two-edge overlap in a block: only $pq$,$cq$.

Both allowed pairs are adjacent. For completeness, in dense case 2 $ac$ with $ae$ requires deleted $ce$; $ac$ with $ad$ requires absent $cd$; $ac$ with $be$ requires absent $ab$; $ae$ with $be$ requires absent $ab$; $ad$ with $be$ requires deleted $bd$. Only $ae$,$ad$ remains, precluding a triple. In dense case 3, the pairs respectively require deleted $ac$, absent $de$, absent $ab$, deleted $ac$, absent $bc$, or deleted $bd$. In dense case 4, every pair except $pq$,$cq$ requires deleted $ap$ or $bq$, or an absent pair among $a$,$b$,$c$. Dense case 1's three pairs require $bc$ or $pq$. These are all pair tests.

### 5.2 Three sparse types

For a bowtie $L=abc\cup ade$, take $M=\{bc,de\}$, $Q=\{a\}$. The cover increment has size three for a compatible two-packing, immediately strict.

For $L=K_{2,3}$ with sides $\{a,b\}$,$\{c,d,e\}$, take $M=\{ac,bd\}$, $Q=\{a,b\}$. An external $acx$ combines with $vad$,$vbe$. The old forbidden edges are $ad$,$be$,$ax$,$cx$. Missing/deleted $ac$,$ab$,$cd$,$ce$ exclude every pair except $ad$,$ax$, adjacent at $a$. The footprint has at most two edges in each block and is a star, so Lemma 2A excludes an external $ac$-page; symmetry handles every rim edge. There are no triangles within $L$, so each rim edge belongs only to its $v$-triangle, contradicting Section 3.

For $L=C_5$ with rim $abcde$, take $M=\{ab,cd\}$, $Q=\{c,e\}$. An external $abx$ combines with $vbc$,$vde$. Old forbidden edges are $bc$,$de$,$ax$,$bx$. Deleted $ab$,$cd$ and absent $ad$,$bd$ leave only the possible pair $bc$,$bx$. The footprint in each block is a star of size at most two. Lemma 2A excludes such an external page, and symmetry excludes all rim pages. Again each rim edge belongs to just its $v$-triangle, contradiction.

### 5.3 The remaining type $K_{2,2,1}$

The local four-triangle/eight-edge witness is Puleo's [2, Proposition 5.1, proof Case 1]; the residual-equality and external-page compatibility extension is proved here.

Write the missing link edges $ab$,$cd$ and the fifth link vertex $e$. The local graph $B$ on $W=\{v,a,b,c,d,e\}$ is $K_6$ minus $ab$,$cd$. Delete all $B$-edges to $K$. The four edge-disjoint triangles $vac$,$vbd$,$ade$,$bce$ append to every $K$-packing. All eight rim edges cover every lost triangle through $v$ and every other lost triangle. Hence equality forces $\nu(K)=h-4$ and $\tau(K)=2h-8$, and $K$ has equality blocks. Each block meets $W$ at most once, since $W$ is independent in $K$.

Let $F$ be the external rim pages, triangles with a rim edge and apex outside $W$. The lost triangles are exactly the $B$-triangles and $F$. $B$ has the four-edge cover $\{va,vb,ec,ed\}$; therefore equality forces $\tau(F)\ge 4$.

Call the following four pairs of rim edges bad:


$$
\{ac,bd\}, \{ad,bc\}, \{ae,be\}, \{ce,de\}
$$


These four bad pairs form a perfect matching on the eight rim edges: every rim edge has exactly one bad partner. A third, distinct base is therefore good with both members of a bad pair.

Every other pair $f$,$g$ is good and $B-\{f,g\}$ has three edge-disjoint triangles. The symmetries swapping $a$,$b$, swapping $c$,$d$ and exchanging the two two-vertex parts reduce all good pairs to four cases:

| $f$,$g$ | Three triangles avoiding them |
|---|---|
| $ac$,$ad$ | $vae$; $bce$; $vbd$ |
| $ae$,$ce$ | $bde$; $vad$; $vbc$ |
| $ac$,$ae$ | $bde$; $vad$; $vbc$ |
| $ac$,$be$ | $ade$; $vbd$; $vce$ |

The four cases are adjacent pairs of cycle edges, spokes at $e$ to different parts, an incident mixed pair, and a nonincident mixed pair. The remaining cycle pairs and spoke pairs are precisely those listed as bad. Thus the list covers every good pair without an appeal to enumeration.

If $F$ has no edge-disjoint pair on good bases, then $\tau(F)\le 2$. To prove this, an intersecting $F$ already has a two-edge cover. Otherwise choose disjoint pages on bases $f$,$g$, which must be bad partners. Every page on a third base must intersect both, since a third base is good with each bad partner. Such intersections require a common external apex and bases meeting both $f$ and $g$.

For adjacent bad partners $ae$,$be$ (or $ce$,$de$), disjointness requires distinct apices, so no third base occurs; $f$,$g$ cover $F$. The same holds for disjoint partners with distinct apices. For disjoint partners $ac$,$bd$ with common apex $x$, a third base meeting both is only $ad$ or $bc$, and its page has apex $x$. Its presence forces every page on $ac$ or $bd$ to have apex $x$, or else it would form a good disjoint pair with that third page. The other possible third base likewise has apex $x$. Thus $F$ lies in the four pages at $x$ over the cycle $ac$,$cb$,$bd$,$da$, covered by $xa$,$xb$. If there is no third base, $ac$,$bd$ cover $F$. This proves the claim; symmetry handles $ad$,$bc$.

Since $\tau(F)\ge 4$, $F$ has a disjoint pair on good bases $f$,$g$. Combine these two pages with the displayed local three-packing avoiding $f$,$g$. Each residual block meets $W$ at most once, and hence meets each external page in at most one old spoke. If it meets both, the forbidden spokes share its unique $W$ vertex. The local three-packing has no surviving edges because all $B$-edges were deleted. Thus the entire footprint is the indicated star of at most two spokes, including for $K_5$. Lemma 2A appends all five selected triangles, yielding $h+1$, contradiction.

This completes exclusion of every 3-colorable five-vertex link component.

### 5.4 One additional non-3-colorable link

The link consisting of $K_4$ on $a$,$b$,$c$,$d$ and a fifth vertex $x$ adjacent exactly to $a$,$b$ is also excluded. Take $M=\{cd,ax\}$ and $Q=\{a,b\}$; $L-Q$ is the single edge $cd$. Deleting the local $v$-spokes and $M$ forces equality blocks with packing $h-2$. The triangles $acd$,$vax$,$vbd$ are edge-disjoint and have old forbidden edges $ac$,$ad$,$bd$. A block cannot contain both $ac$,$ad$ or both $ac$,$bd$ because $cd$ is deleted; the only possible pair is $ad$,$bd$, adjacent at $d$. The entire footprint is consequently a star with at most two edges. Lemma 2A appends the three triangles, giving $h+1$, contradiction.

### 5.5 The two remaining degree-five links

Every $K_4$-free graph on at most five vertices is 3-colorable. Indeed, a vertex-minimal graph that is not 3-colorable has minimum degree at least 3. On four vertices it is $K_4$; on five its complement is a matching. $K_5$ minus zero or one edge contains $K_4$, while $K_5$ minus two independent edges is $K_{2,2,1}$ and is 3-colorable.

Thus a degree-five link not already excluded contains $K_4$. Its fifth vertex has at least two neighbors there. Exactly two is the configuration excluded in Section 5.4; three gives $K_5$ minus one edge, and four gives $K_5$. Hence every degree-five vertex of a minimal $S$ obstruction has one of these two links.

## 6. Degree-five vertices are independent and have no degree-six neighbor

**Lemma 7 (Low-neighbor restriction).** Degree-five vertices form an independent set in a minimal combined obstruction, and every neighbor of such a vertex has degree at least seven.

*Proof.*

**Attribution and extension.** The following packing/cover accounting is Puleo's reducible-set framework (Definition 2.1, Lemma 2.2). His Proposition 5.2 is the antecedent for low-degree adjacency, including the precise balanced witnesses in Section 6.2. For the combined obstruction, only a strict reduction is an immediate contradiction. Every balanced case below explicitly supplies the additional equality argument.

We use the reducible-set instance of Lemma 3A with the actual packing and cover witnesses displayed in each case. A strict cover bound contradicts that lemma; a balanced bound yields its exact residual equality and classification.

The singleton matching version takes a matching $M$ in a link and a vertex set $Q$ such that the link minus $Q$ is a subgraph of $M$. Delete the central vertex and $M$. The hub triangles on $M$ give $|M|$ packed triangles, and $M$ plus the spokes to $Q$ give a cover increment $|M|+|Q|$. The set $Q$ may contain endpoints of edges in $M$.

**Residual-support observation.** In each application, the residual graph $K$ has a five-vertex set $R$ such that $K[R]$ is $K_5$ with one edge or two independent edges deleted. These deleted pairs are nonedges of $K$. In each such induced graph all remaining edges lie in one triangle component with five vertices. It cannot lie in a $K_4$ block; it cannot lie in a $K_5$ block because the specified missing edge was deleted from the whole residual. This can also be seen by listing their triangles or starting with two overlapping $K_4$ copies in the one-edge case.

### 6.1 Dominating neighbors of degree five or six

Let $v$ have degree 5 and let $u$ be a neighbor with $N[v]\subseteq N[u]$. Write $W=N(v)-\{u\}$, $B=G[\{u,v\}\cup W]$, and $Z=N(u)-N[v]$. Then $B$ is $K_6$ or $K_6$ minus one rim edge, and $|Z|=d(u)-5$.

Take $X=E(G[W])\cup \{uv\}\cup \{uz:z\in Z\}$. It meets every triangle at $u$ or $v$. If $B$ is $K_6-ab$ and $|Z|\le 1$, $X$ has at most 7 edges and $B$ has the four-packing $auv$,$acd$,$bud$,$bcv$ ($W=\{a,b,c,d\}$); this is strict. If $B=K_6$ and $Z$ is empty, $|X|=7$ and again a four-packing is strict.

If $B=K_6$ and $Z=\{p\}$, the edge $up$ belongs to a triangle, so $p$ has a neighbor $w$ in $W$ ($v$ has no neighbor $p$). Choose a four-packing of $K_6$ avoiding $uw$ and add $upw$. Add $pw$ to $X$. Its size is $9<10$, strict. The required four-packing exists because $K_6$ minus a perfect matching decomposes into four triangles: for nonedge pairs $ab$,$cd$,$st$, use $acs$,$adt$,$bct$,$bds$; extend $uw$ to such a matching.

Thus no dominating neighbor of a degree-five vertex has degree 5 or 6.

### 6.2 Adjacent degree-five vertices

If two degree-five vertices $u$,$v$ are adjacent and have four common neighbors, they dominate each other and Section 6.1 applies. Otherwise, their precise links force three common neighbors $W=\{w_1,w_2,w_3\}$. Both links are $K_5$ minus one edge. Let $p$ be the unique neighbor of $u$ outside $N[v]$ and $q$ the unique neighbor of $v$ outside $N[u]$. The vertices $p$,$q$ are distinct, each joins all of $W$, $vp$ and $uq$ are absent, and $W$ is a triangle. Whether $pq$ is present is irrelevant.

Use


$$
P=\{uw_1w_2, vw_1w_3, upw_3, vqw_2\},
$$


$$
X=E(W)\cup \{uv,up,vq,pw_3,qw_2\}
$$


This is a balanced four/eight reduction deleting $u$,$v$. Its residual $K$ has equality blocks and $W$ is independent there. The five triangles


$$
uvw_1, upw_2, vqw_3, pw_1w_3, qw_1w_2
$$


are edge-disjoint. Their surviving edges in $K$ are exactly $pw_1$,$pw_2$,$qw_1$,$qw_3$. A residual block meets $W$ at most once, so its whole surviving footprint has at most two edges sharing that vertex. Lemma 2A appends all five triangles, contradiction. Hence the degree-five vertices form an independent set.

### 6.3 A nondominating degree-six neighbor

Suppose $v$ has degree 5 with link $K_5-ut$, and $u$ is one of the missing-edge endpoints. Thus $N(v)=\{u,t,a,b,c\}$, $ut$ is absent, and $W=\{a,b,c\}$ is a triangle. If $d(u)=6$, write its two remaining neighbors $p$,$q$ outside $N[v]$. In $G-u$, the vertices $\{v,t,a,b,c\}$ induce $K_5$.

If $pq$ is present, in the link at $u$ take $M=\{pq,va,bc\}$ and $Q=W$. Outside $Q$ the only link edge is $pq$. This balanced three/six singleton reduction leaves that $K_5$ minus the two independent edges $va$,$bc$, impossible for residual equality blocks.

If $pq$ is absent, triangle codegree at least 2 for $up$ and $uq$ implies that $p$,$q$ each have at least two neighbors in $W$. Choose distinct $a\in N(p)\cap W$ and $b\in N(q)\cap W$, with $c$ the third vertex. Take $M=\{pa,qb,vc\}$ and $Q=W$. The link outside $Q$ is independent. This balanced three/six reduction leaves the $K_5$ with only $vc$ deleted, again impossible.

Together with the minimum-degree bound in Lemma 5 and Sections 6.1–6.2, this proves:

**Low-neighbor restriction.** Every neighbor of a degree-five vertex has degree at least 7.

## 7. Overlap restriction for nonadjacent degree-five vertices

**Proposition 8 (Overlap restriction; Proposition $O$).** Two nonadjacent degree-five vertices in a minimal combined obstruction have at most three common neighbors. If they have three, both links are $K_5$.

*Proof.*

**Attribution and extension.** Botler–Fernandes–Gutiérrez Lemma 3.3 proves the corresponding implication in irreducible robust graphs: degrees at most six and a neighborhood union of size at most seven force both degrees to be five, an intersection of size three, and both links $K_5$. For two degree-five vertices, an intersection of at least three meets that union hypothesis. Its balanced reductions cannot simply exclude a minimal combined-$S$ failure. The residual-block arguments in Sections 7.2–7.4 discharge that extra requirement; this is the precise distinction between the predecessor and the version needed here.

Write $C=N(x)\cap N(y)$. The two links are $K_5$ or $K_5$ minus one edge by Section 5. No assumption is made about other degrees.

### 7.1 Five common neighbors

Their common neighborhood A has five vertices and is $K_5$ or $K_5-ab$. Delete $x$,$y$ and $E(A)$; the cover increment is $|E(A)|$.

When $A=K_5$ on $\{a,b,c,d,e\}$, the six triangles
$xbc$, $xde$, $ybd$, $yce$, $abe$, $acd$
are disjoint. The cover increment ten is strictly smaller than twelve.

When $A=K_5-ab$, omit $abe$ from that list. The remaining five triangles exist and the cover increment nine is strictly smaller than ten.

### 7.2 Four common neighbors

Write $W=C$ and let $p$,$q$ be the respective unique neighbors outside the common neighborhood. The graph on $W$ is $K_4$ or $K_4$ minus one edge. It has two edge-disjoint perfect matchings, so four triangles, two at each center, form a packing.

Take $X=E(W)\cup \{xp,yq\}$. It meets all triangles at $x$,$y$ and contains the noncentral edges of this four-packing. If $W$ has five edges this is strict, with $|X|=7$.

If $W=K_4$, the reduction is balanced four/eight and the residual has equality blocks with $W$ independent. The vertex $p$ has at least three neighbors in $W$, because the link at $x$ misses at most one edge. Thus there is a page $p$ $f$ on some $W$-edge $f$. The graph on $\{x,y\}\cup W$ is $K_6-xy$. Since $xy$ and $f$ are disjoint, it has a four-packing avoiding $f$. The local four-packing has no surviving residual edges: all its edges are incident with $x,y$ or lie in $W$. A residual block meets the independent set $W$ at most once, so the page contributes at most one surviving spoke. Thus the whole footprint is a star of size at most one, also below the $K_5$ two-edge bound. Lemma 2A appends the page and four-packing, giving $\nu(G)+1$, a contradiction.

### 7.3 Three common neighbors, a missing edge inside $C$

If a common edge $ac$ is absent, write $C=\{a,b,c\}$, $N(x)-C=\{p,q\}$, $N(y)-C=\{r,s\}$. Both links are precisely $K_5-ac$; all edges required below therefore exist. The pairs $p$,$q$ and $r,s$ are disjoint, because $C$ is exactly the common neighborhood.

Use
$P=\{qab,bcr,xpa,xqc,yar,ycs\}$
and
$X=E(qab)\cup E(bcr)\cup \{qc,pa,ar,cs,xp,ys\}$.
The six triangles are disjoint and $|X|=12$. It covers every triangle incident to $x$ or $y$: $xp$ handles the $p$-pages at $x$, $qa$,$qb$,$qc$ handle its $q$-pages, $ab$,$bc$ handle its $C$-triangles; the $y$ side is analogous. Every noncentral $P$-edge lies in $X$. Thus the residual has equality blocks.

Now use the seven edge-disjoint triangles
$xpa$, $qab$, $pbc$, $xqc$, $yar$, $ysb$, $rsc$.
Their edges surviving in the residual are exactly $pb$,$pc$,$sb$,$rs$. Every pair of these except $pb$,$sb$ requires an absent residual edge to be in a common clique block: $pb$/$pc$ requires $bc$, $sb$/$rs$ requires $br$, $pb$/$rs$ requires $br$, $pc$/$sb$ requires $bc$, and $pc$/$rs$ requires $cr$. Those edges were deleted. Hence each block contains at most two forbidden edges and the only possible pair shares $b$. The entire footprint therefore meets both hypotheses of Lemma 2A, which appends the seven-packing, contradiction.

### 7.4 Three common neighbors, a missing edge outside $C$

Suppose $C$ is a triangle and at least one link is $K_5$ minus an edge; take that link to be the one at $y$. Let its missing edge be $e$. At least one endpoint of $e$ lies outside $C$. Choose an edge $f=ac$ of $C$ disjoint from $e$ and let $b$ be the third vertex.

Write $N(x)-C=\{p,q\}$. At least one of $p$,$q$ joins all three $C$ vertices; call it $p$. Relabel $a$,$c$ if necessary so that $qa$ exists. Then $pb$ also exists.

The core on $\{y\}\cup N(y)$ is $K_6-e$. Because $e$ and $f$ are disjoint, it has a four-packing $P_0$ avoiding $f$. Take
$P=P_0\cup \{xac,xpb\}$
and
$X=E(G[N(y)])\cup \{xp,xq,pb\}$.
This is a balanced six/twelve reduction deleting $x$,$y$. The nine edges of the near-clique link at $y$ cover all its triangles. Any $x$-triangle either contains $p$ or $q$, hit by $xp$ or $xq$, or has its other two vertices in $C$, whose edges are deleted. Noncentral packed edges all lie in $X$.

The residual has equality blocks and $N(y)$ is independent in it. Replace the two $x$-triangles by three triangles
$pac$, $xpb$, $xqa$.
Together with $P_0$ they form a seven-packing. Its surviving edges are $pa$,$pc$,$qa$: $pb$ and $ac$ were deleted. A residual block meets $N(y)$ at most once, so the whole footprint has at most two edges, with the only possible pair $pa$,$qa$, sharing $a$. Lemma 2A gives the contradiction.

All cases with a near-clique link are excluded, proving Proposition $O$.

## 8. The global peeling reduction and final local configuration

**Lemma 9 (Final configuration and exclusion).** A five-degenerate minimal combined obstruction forces the eight-vertex configuration described below, with arbitrary outside attachments, and this configuration cannot occur.

*Proof.*

We now exclude the minimal obstruction in the subgraph-closed class of all 5-degenerate graphs.

Let $G$ be a minimal $S$ failure among 5-degenerate graphs. Let $L$ be its set of degree-five vertices. It is nonempty by degeneracy and Section 4. Section 6 makes $L$ independent and gives degree at least 7 for all its neighbors.

The subgraph $G-L$ is nonempty and 5-degenerate. Choose $u$ in it with at most five neighbors in $G-L$. Set $A=N(u)-L$, $D=d(u)$, $r=|N(u)\cap L|$. Then $|A|\le 5$ and $r\ge D-5$. Since $u$ is outside $L$ and $\delta(G)\ge 5$, $D\ge 6$, so $r\ge 1$. Thus $u$ does have a neighbor in $L$, and the low-neighbor restriction gives $D\ge 7$ and $r\ge 2$.

For each $v$ in $N(u)\cap L$, put $A_v=N(v)\cap A$. If $u$ dominates $v$, $|A_v|=4$; otherwise $|A_v|=3$, and $v$ has one further neighbor $p_v$ outside $N[u]$. These descriptions use the precise $K_5$/$K_5$-minus-edge links. For distinct low vertices $v$,$w$, the sets $A_v$,$A_w$ intersect in at most one vertex. Indeed two common $A$ vertices together with $u$ give at least three common neighbors. Proposition $O$ excludes this if either link is a near-clique. If both links are cliques, both $A$ sets have size four in an at-most-five-element set, so their intersection has size at least three and there are at least four common neighbors, again excluded.

There can be at most two subsets of an at-most-five-element set, each of size at least three, whose pairwise intersections have size at most one. To see this, two must each have size three, meet in one point and exhaust five points. Any third three-set would have total intersection size at least three with their union, whereas meeting each in at most one allows at most two. Thus $r=2$, $D=7$, $|A|=5$, and both $A$ sets are triples meeting in exactly one vertex.

Label
$A=\{a,b,c,d,e\}$,
$N(v)=\{u,p,a,b,c\}$,
$N(w)=\{u,q,a,d,e\}$,
$N(u)=\{v,w,a,b,c,d,e\}$.
The low vertices $v$,$w$ have near-clique links missing $up$,$uq$ respectively. The vertices $p$,$q$ lie outside $N[u]$ and are distinct: if they were equal, $v$,$w$ would have three common neighbors $u$,$a$,$p$ and Proposition $O$ would exclude them. The sets $\{a,b,c\}$ and $\{a,d,e\}$ are triangles.

### 8.1 The four cross edges are forced

Suppose one of the four edges joining $\{b,c\}$ to $\{d,e\}$ is absent. Relabel within each pair so that $ce$ is absent.

In the link at $u$, choose $M=\{vc,we,ab\}$, $Q=\{a,b,d\}$. Outside $Q$ the vertices are $v$,$c$,$w$,$e$, whose only edges are $vc$ and $we$: $vw$,$ve$,$wc$ are absent by the displayed neighborhoods and $ce$ is absent by assumption. Hence this is a balanced singleton three/six reduction.

The residual graph induced on $\{v,p,a,b,c\}$ is $K_5$ with $vc$ and $ab$ deleted; both pairs are nonedges of that residual. The other deleted edge $we$ is outside this vertex set because $p$ lies outside $N[u]$. This is impossible for the equality block classification. Thus all four cross edges exist and $A$ is $K_5$.

### 8.2 The final eight-vertex graph $B$

Let $B$ be the graph induced on $\{u,v,w,a,b,c,d,e\}$. It has $A=K_5$, $u$ joined to all other seven vertices, $v$ joined within $B$ precisely to $u$,$a$,$b$,$c$, and $w$ joined within $B$ precisely to $u$,$a$,$d$,$e$. The only further neighbors of $v$,$w$ in $G$ are $p$,$q$ respectively.

![Figure 1. The final eight-vertex core B.](final-core.svg)

**Figure 1.** Exactly the 23 edges of $B$ are drawn. Gray edges give $A=K_5$, dashed red edges join $u$ to the other seven vertices, and teal edges give the two arms at $v,w$. Crossings are not additional vertices. The drawing excludes outside vertices: in $G$, $v,w$ also have the respective neighbors $p,q$, and vertices of $A$ may have unrestricted outside attachments. The displayed local graph does not bound those attachments.

A seven-packing of $B$ avoiding $ab$ is
$vua$, $vbc$, $wud$, $wae$, $uce$, $acd$, $bde$.
The two unused $B$ edges are $ub$,$ab$. By swaps inside $\{b,c\}$, inside $\{d,e\}$, and exchange of the two arms together with $v$,$w$, there is a seven-packing avoiding each $A$-edge incident with $a$.

**Pair-avoidance claim.** For any two distinct $A$-edges $f$,$g$, $B-\{f,g\}$ has six edge-disjoint triangles.

If one edge is incident to $a$, take a seven-packing avoiding it and discard the possible triangle using the other edge. It remains to consider pairs among the six edges on $\{b,c,d,e\}$. Up to the same symmetries their types and witnesses are:

| Avoided edges / type | Six edge-disjoint triangles |
| --- | --- |
| $bc$,$de$: two arm edges | $vub$, $vac$, $wud$, $wae$, $uce$, $abd$ |
| $bc$,$bd$: arm edge and cross edge | $vub$, $vac$, $wue$, $wad$, $ucd$, $abe$ |
| $bd$,$ce$: disjoint cross edges | $vub$, $vac$, $wue$, $wad$, $ucd$, $abe$ |
| $bd$,$be$: adjacent cross edges | $vua$, $vbc$, $wud$, $wae$, $uce$, $acd$ |

These four cases exhaust pairs: an arm edge and any cross edge meet; two cross edges either meet or are disjoint. Every displayed triangle uses only $B$ edges and the triangles in each row are pairwise edge-disjoint. Thus this is an ordinary finite certificate with an explicit symmetry reduction, not an appeal to an unperformed enumeration.

### 8.3 External-page augmentation closes the configuration

Delete $u$,$v$,$w$ and every $A$-edge, obtaining $K$. The seven-packing of $B$ appends to every $K$-packing. The fourteen edges
$X=E(A)\cup \{uv,uw,vp,wq\}$
cover every triangle lost in the deletion. Triangles at $u$ are inside $B$; triangles at $v$ or $w$ are inside $B$ or use $vp$ or $wq$; other lost triangles use an $A$-edge. Equality therefore forces
$\nu(K)=\nu(G)-7$, $\tau(K)=2\nu(K)$,
and $K$ has $K_4$/$K_5$ triangle components. Since $A$ is independent in $K$, each block meets A at most once.

Let $F$ be the family of all triangles with an $A$-edge as base and apex outside $B$. If $F$ contains two edge-disjoint members on bases $f$,$g$, use a six-packing of $B$ avoiding $f$,$g$ and append those two pages. The local six-packing has no edges in $K$. Each page contributes at most one surviving spoke to a residual block, because its two base endpoints lie in the independent set $A$. Thus the whole footprint is a star at the block's unique $A$ vertex and has at most two edges, including for a $K_5$ block. Lemma 2A applies. This constructs $\nu(K)+8=\nu(G)+1$ triangles, contradiction.

Thus $F$ is pairwise edge-intersecting and has a cover of size at most two by the elementary intersecting-triangle lemma.

The following nine edges cover $B$:
$\{ua,ub,ab,cd,ce,de,vc,wd,we\}$.
The first six are the within-part edges of the $3+3$ partition $\{u,a,b\}$/$\{c,d,e\}$ of the $K_6$ core. The only remaining $v$-triangles use $vc$; the only remaining $w$-triangles use $wd$ or $we$.

There are four separate cover contributions:

1. A minimum $K$-cover handles all triangles surviving in $K$.
2. The displayed nine-edge cover handles all triangles wholly in $B$.
3. An $F$-cover of size at most two handles all triangles with an $A$-edge and apex outside $B$.
4. The two edges $vp$,$wq$ handle every remaining triangle incident with the deleted low vertices $v$,$w$.

To check exhaustiveness, a lost triangle either meets $\{u,v,w\}$ or uses a deleted $A$-edge. Any triangle at $u$ is wholly in $B$ because $N(u)=\{v,w\}\cup A$. A triangle at $v$ either lies in $B$ or uses its unique outside-neighbor edge $vp$; similarly $w$ and $wq$. A triangle using an $A$-edge either has its third vertex in $B$, or is an external page in $F$. All graph edges chosen in the $F$-cover are actual edges of $G$. Contributions can overlap, which only reduces the size of their union; no disjointness is needed for the upper bound. Thus a minimum $K$-cover plus the other contributions has size at most $\tau(K)+9+2+2=\tau(K)+13$, contradicting $\tau(G)=\tau(K)+14$.

For the inequality alone, the earlier seven/fourteen reducing tuple already contradicts irreducibility, as reconstructed in the short credited proof. The saving from fourteen to thirteen and the argument for arbitrary outside pages are retained here to exclude equality obstructions.

Therefore the minimal failure cannot exist.

## 9. Conclusion, converse and scope

The class of finite 5-degenerate graphs is closed under every vertex and edge deletion used above. If it contained a failure of $S$, choose one with the fewest edges and discard isolates. Sections 1–5 give the minimal-obstruction premises. Sections 6–8 exclude it. Hence every graph in this class satisfies the inequality and the asserted necessity at equality.

Conversely, packing and covering numbers add over triangle components because their edge supports are disjoint. $K_4$ has $(\nu,\tau)=(1,2)$, $K_5$ has (2,4), and triangle-free edges contribute zero. Thus the stated component condition implies equality, including the vacuous triangle-free case.

This proves the main theorem by ordinary finite graph arguments. The formal-verification account appears in Section 10; the ordinary argument and finite checks have distinct evidentiary roles. No external human endorsement or established historical priority is claimed.

For an individual graph independently known to be 5-degenerate, this theorem supplies Tuza's inequality and the stated equality characterization. No unrestricted restoration, strictness, OCT-five, or density-class theorem is established here. Here OCT-five means the class of graphs made bipartite by deleting at most five vertices; no assertion for that entire class follows from the degeneracy theorem.
